6. Taken into account the documents and other material made available to it and oral evidence tendered before 
it the Committee concludes as under :-
6.01 The Performance Budget of the Ministry of Mines for the year 1994-95 states that the Ministry is 
primarily responsible for the regulation and development of the mineral sector including the mining and 
metallurgy of all non ferrous metals both in private and public sectors but excluding Natural Gas , Petroleum 
coal and Atomic minerals. Mmeral resources are national assets. Conservation and planned exploitation of 
minerals are therefore, of prime importance to the national economy. Besides providing the basic inputs to 
domestic industry the mineral sector accounts for sizeable exports and foreign exchange earni ngs. Having 
regard to the extent and variety of mineral resources in the country there is great potential for rapid growth 
of this sector. It is the onus of the. Ministry of the Mines to develop this sector with utmost care and caution 
to enable this sector to compete with the contemporary globalisation in the internatio nal area. But the 
Committee finds that the entire mines and minerals sector is in doldrums. Large number of mines have either 
closed or at the brink of closure. The situation is very alarming particularl y in the States of Bihar , Andhra 
Pradesh , Rajasthan, Goa, Orissa, Madhya Pradesh etc. where a good number of Mines have closed dov·m. 
There is no provision in the Demands for Grants of the Ministry for the revival of closed Mines in the 
country. The Committee has not been told of any kind of package prepared by the Ministry for the reopening 
of closed mines in the country and make them viable. Rather the Committee has been told that the minerals 
belong to the State Governments. The onus of re-opening of closed mines is therefore the responsibility of 
the States and Ministry has washed its hands off by pointing out the responsibihty on the States ignoring 
the loss being caused to the nation due to the closure of mines throughout the country. The States faced with 
acute resource constraints and are unable to divert their attention towards the closed· mines. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government must also pay attention towards the closed/ 
closing mines throughout the country and prepare a comprehensive package for their revival in 
consultation with the State Governments concerned. There must be a perfect co-ordi nation between 

2 
the Governme nt and the Gove rnm ent of the States in thi s •·egard . The Governm ent should constitut e 
a tea m of experts to find out the causes of closure of mines and suggest the ways for their revival within 
a t ime frame. 
6.02 The Committee finds that there is lack of coordination between the Government and the Government 
of the States as far as regulating of mining is concerned. Responding to a query about the foreign investment 
in the mineral sector after the enactment of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) 
Amendment Act, 1994 the Secretary of Ministry of Mines states that the minerals belong to the State 
Governmen ts. All applicat ions have to be submitted by entrepreneurs to the concerned State Governments 
and it is they who have to give the prospecting licence or the mining lease as the case may be. The 
Government did not have precise information whether any State Government had received any formal 
proposa l and whether any foreign party has applied for any prospecting licence. The Committee finds it not 
convincing. After opening the mineral sector of the country for foreign investment and participation in order 
to accelerating i nflow of domestic and foreign capita l into the mineral sector the Governme nt has left the 
matter entirely to the State Governments. On such a vital issue there should have been a perfect 
understanding and coordination between the Central and State Governments. The Committ ee, ther efor e, 
recommends· that Governm ent must keep a watch on every foreign investment propo sal in the miner al 
sector and advi se the c once rn ed State Government to make best u se of such a propo sal with out 
compr omising nationa l interest and prioritie s and maintain the closest coordin ation with the State 
Govern ment in thi s regar d. If there are stron g sentiment s expr essed by the State Gove rnmen t, as far 
as possib le such sentiments should be respecte d. It is import ant th at compensation money reac hes the 
peo ple allocated to Geological Survey of India (GSI) in Major Head 2853. GS I plays a dominant role for 
the gro\\th of the Mineral sector of the country. According to the Perforn1ance Budget (1994- 95) of the 
Ministry GSI is responsible for collection. collation and dissemination of geological data and providing 
basic geologic~ I information essential for the successful implementation of practically are the developmen­
tal programmes of the count!). The investigation carried out by GSI contribute directly to the discovery and 
evaluation of mineral resources ensuring thereby the continued and steady supply of vital ra\\ materials to 
the core industrial sector . The results of investigation aid in the better understanding of the cmstal 
framework and the geological process with bearing on development in other as vital sectors such as 
agriculture, land use management, irrigation and power development. utilisation of water resources. 
development of transport and communication, educat ion and scientific management of environment. Thus 
survey and mapping and mineral exploration are the most important functions ofGSI for Mineral sector 
and geological process having bearing on other important sectors oft he country but the committee finds that 
out of the total allocation ofRs. 125.74% crores in BE 1994-95 only a sum ofRs. 11.20 crorcs has been 
earmarked for survey and mapping and Rs. 12.90 for mineral exploration. Thus a total sum ofRs. 25.10 
crores will be spent on the vital functions of Survey and mapping and Mineral exploration whereas more 
than Rs. I 00 crores will be spent on other purposes mainly administration etc. The committee, therefore, 
recommends that additional funds be allocated for such primary functio ns as survey and mapping and 
Mineral exploration of the GSI. Such Su rveys and exp lorat ion should conform to a precise ly ind icated 
time frame so that a check would be possib le on tangible res ults achieved. The Committee appreciates 
the gesture of the Government in increasing the resource Budgetary allocation to GSI as per its 
recommendations made in its Thjrd Report on the Demands for Grants of the Ministl) ' of Mines ( 1993-94 ). 
However, the Committee recommends that instead of allocating a substa ntial amou nt for other 
purposes to GSI more thr ust should be given for its basic work. T hough the GSI is achieving its 
ta r gets, additiona l resources will certain ly bring an improveme nt in basic work and the nat ion will 
be benefitted.

confidence in the PS Us functioning under the jurisdiction on his M inistl) "hich inspite of a lot of pressure 
are doing quite \\ell. Citing an e-.:ample he stated that BALCO has recorded a profit of almost two and a

REPORT
 
National Mineral Development Corporation Limited (NMDC) , a Government of India Enterprise and  a “Mini
Ratna Category-I” Company was established  in the year 1958, in pursuance of Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 to
promote and undertake development of minerals (other than coal, oil and atomic minerals) in Public Sector. NMDC is
the largest producer and exporter of iron ore in this Country. Its exports are around 7 million tonnes of iron ore per
annum (through Minerals & Metals Trading Corporation Ltd - canalising agency). It has also exported about 1.7 MT of

of foreign exchange. NMDC has been consistently achieving the rating of “ Excellent” from the very first year of
signing the MoU viz 1991-92.  It was placed in the fourth rank amongst the MOU signing PSEs for the year 1991-92,

1999-2000, 2000-2001 and 2001-2002 NMDC was adjudged “Excellent”, barring 1998-99 during which period there
was general recession.

8.1       Iron ore Mining: NMDC Management is always in search of latest Mining technology and equipment.
Accordingly, higher capacity drills, shovels and dumpers have been deployed in various existing Mines. In new Mines
120 ton capacity Dumpers against 50 T Dumpers and 8 meter cube Shovels against 4.6 meter cube Shovels and single
pass Drills against multi pass Drills are being planned. Latest information technology is being adopted in OCSL Plant
like; PLC, CCTV etc. The modern technology will enhance the productivity of Mines and also will result in reduction in
cost.
 
8.2       Diamond Mining: Mechanised Diamond Mine at Majghawan had a capacity of 24,480 carats per year by
adopting jigging technology. By adopting latest heavy media separation and X-ray sorting machinery, capacity of the
Mine has been enhanced to 84000 carats per year.  During the year 2001-02 the Mine could achieve 81,100 carats of
production. This has resulted in reduction in cost of production.
 
8.3       NMDC has identified the ROMELT technology of Russia which can  make use of low grade iron ore slimes to
convert  into pig iron. The technology has not so far been commercially used and NMDC would be the first Company in
the world to use ROMELT technology on a commercial basis in Bailadila Sector at an estimated cost of Rs.300 crores
including Rs.20 crores as loan from Technical Development Board, Govt. of India.  The ROMELT SAIL India Ltd

10.0     COST COMPONENTS OF PRODUCTS PRODUCEDBY NMDC .
 
10.1     The main components of the cost of production are  Fixed Cost and  Variable Cost.
The fixed cost consists of salaries and wages, depreciation and office/ selling expenses. The fixed cost is being reduced
by introduction of multi-skilling concepts and by adoption of CCTV at OCSL Plants. The variable cost consists of
explosives, drill bits, tyre & tubes, spares and consumables. It also consists cost incurred towards royalty and
electricity. 
 
10.2     The cost of production at pit head is comparable with the International Mining Operations. NMDC has to incur
additional Railway freight and Port handling charges  before product reaches the consumer. The port charges and
Railway freight charges are not under the control of NMDC. It may be worth mentioning that the cost incurred in
Railway freight and port charges amounts to 60% of the cost and balance 40% cost is in the control of NMDC. This
situation creates difficulty for NMDC to compete in the  international market for iron ore. Unless efforts are made to
reduce the railway freight and port charges, it will be difficult for NMDC to sustain the progress of the Corporation. 
 
10.3     Continuous efforts are being made towards cost reduction through the various managerial controls such as

       Bench Marking

c.       Standard Costing
d.      Continuous review of consumables and improvement in the same

12.0     MOU RATING OF NMDC 
 
12.1     NMDC is one of the Public Sector Enterprises which has been signing Memorandum of Understanding (MoU)
with the Government of India since 1991. At the beginning of each financial year, an agreement is reached to achieve
certain parameters such as production, sales, gross margin, ratio of net profit to capital employed, energy conservation,
R & D efforts, human resource development, project implementation etc. based on the past performance into account,
the growth need and the potential to achieve such levels of performance.  These achievements at the year end are
evaluated for the said parameters and the company gets ranked based on the evaluation score. NMDC has been
consistently achieving the rating of “ EXCELLENT” from the very first year of signing the MoU viz 1991-92.  It was
placed in the fourth rank amongst the MOU signing PSEs for the year 1991-92, from which it moved to third rank in the
year 1992-93.  For the years 1993-94, 1994-95 and 1995-96, for NMDC’s performance of excellence and the
achievement of composite score of 1.00 in each of these years under the MOU performance evaluation, NMDC has
been placed as the ‘ Joint Top Rank PSE’ in the country. This has been a unique achievement as the Joint Top Rank  
has been achieved continuously for three years in succession.  Again, in 1996-97, 1997-98, 1999-2000, 2000-2001 and
2001-2002 NMDC was adjudged “EXCELLENT”, barring 1998-99 during which period there was general recession. 
NMDC had been setting new records of performance in the areas of production, despatches of iron ore, production and
sales of diamonds, profits, increased supplies to domestic consumers.  Thus, NMDC has been consistently scaling new
heights of achievements from year to year both in physical and financial terms including foreign exchange earnings to
the country.   For the year 2001-2002, the company has surpassed the MOU target of dispatches of 180 lakh tonnes of
iron ore by achieving 182.04 lakh tonnes. The company has achieved an ever highest profit before tax of Rs.320.15
crores during 2001-2002.

19.0     LEGAL FRAMEWORK  FOR GROWTH AND DEVELOPMENT OF MINING         OPERATION.
 
19.1     To what extent the existing legal framework is conducive to the growth and development of mining operation.
Any suggestion on the part of NMDC management for legal reform in this regard is as follow:-
 
“Mineral industry is governed by certain statutory act and rules such  as  Mines and Mineral Development and
Regulation Act, Mineral Conservation and Development Rules,  Mineral Concession Rule, , Mines Act etc.  With the 
economic liberalization, a new National  Mineral Policy  was announced in 1993 in which 13  major minerals were
dereserved and also foreign investment in the mineral industry was encouraged.  With the existing change in the legal
frame work, State Governments have been empowered to grant and renew mining lease as  minerals are considered to
be property of  the  concerned States.  However, it is observed that State Govts. are imposing their own conditions in
granting of mining lease and this is causing hindrance in the systematic development of mineral industry.  State
Governments should be advised to  form uniform policy and grant mining/prospecting lease on first come first basis,
rather than tendering, asking  for  additional royalty etc.
 
19.2     Ministry of Mines in consultation with GSI & IBM identify mineral zones, which should be developed to meet
the country’s need and such mineral zones, which should be developed to meet the country’s need and such mineral
zones should be taken out from the purview of Forest Conservation Act. “
 
19.3     The Committee is anguished  to  note the  submission of NMDC management  that  State Govts. are imposing
their own conditions in granting of mining lease and this is causing hindrance in the systematic development of mineral
industry and asking  for sweet equity, additional royalty etc.
 
 
 
19.4     The Committee is of the view that  procedural hurdles and bureaucratic rest-redtapism  should not  come onto
the way of systematic development of mineral industry.
 
19.5     The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Steel should   approach the Department of Mines for
organizing  across the  table interaction of representatives of   mineral enterprises and  officials of state  Government  to
form uniform mineral policy as per the canons of National Mineral Policy 1993 and  sort out problems relating  to
granting of  mining/prospecting lease etc.    The Committee  feels that the Department of Mines should  issue direction 
to GSI and IBM for identification of `Exclusive Mineral Zones’ for systematic exploration and exploitation of  Mineral
resources.  Having been give due weightage  to environmental aspects, `exclusive Mineral zones may be taken out from
the  purview of forest   conservation Act.

21.0     'Pricing policy' of NMDC
 
21.1     NMDC is supplying iron ore in the domestic market as well as for export purposes.  The iron ore, which is
surplus to the domestic demand, is exported to countries like Japan, China and South Korea.  The main export of
NMDC’s ore is through MMTC as per the existing EXIM policy.  However, NMDC is also exporting small quantities of
iron ore directly based on the specific export license issued by the Ministry of Commerce / DGFT.
 
21.2     Export Prices ; The prices for export of iron ore are basically determined by the global demand and supply
position on year-to-year basis. The percentage increase/decrease in prices over the previous year is usually finalized
between the major exporters of iron ore like Australia and Brazil and major importers like Japan and European
countries.  The same percentage increase/decrease in prices is made applicable to the exports from India.  Consequently
the prices of NMDC iron ore is also decided on the same basis. 
           
21.3     Domestic Prices: The despatches to domestic market accounts for about 53% of the total dispatches of NMDC’s
iron ore.  The dispatches to domestic market are regulated in terms of long-term agreement signed by various domestic
customers.  The duration of the agreement is for a maximum period of 5 years.  Iron ore market has remained basically a
buyers market due to frequent and prolonged recessionary trends in the steel industry.  Therefore the fixed escalation in
prices is not the acceptable norm in the industry.  In terms of the long-term agreement the prices of iron ore are to be
settled each year by mutual discussions.  The mutual discussions to finalise the prices instills a sense of confidence
among the buyers that NMDC is sensitive to the customer’s needs.
 
21.4     The Board of Directors of NMDC delegated the powers for deciding the pricing through an internal committee
consisting of CMD, Director (Prdn), Director (Fin) and ED (Comml.) and authorizing CMD to take up action as deemed
necessary in this regard.
21.,5    In terms of the above decision of the Board, negotiations are held by NMDC with the parties concerned in the
beginning of the each financial year.  The negotiation are primarily based upon the “what the market can bear” criteria,
and the ground realities of steel sector.  The negotiation also to some extent take into consideration the global
demand/supply position and trends of iron ore prices in the international market. 
 
21.6     The prices so negotiated and finalized with the parties are put up for the information of the Board and adopted
for supplies during the relevant year.

 21.11.0           NEED OF   AUTONOMY FOR  NMDC IN EXPORT PROMOTION I.E.                               
DIRECT EXPORT BY NMDC
 
 
 21.11.1 The export of iron ore produced by NMDC is canalized through MMTC Ltd. in terms of the existing EXIM
policy.  The iron ore which is surplus to the demand of domestic industry is offered for export.  The major chunk of
export is canalised through MMTC and balance uncommitted quantity is permitted for exports directly by NMDC
through special export license.  The inherent drawback of the system are as follows:
 
                        (i)      The licenses issued to NMDC for exports by DGFT do not permit export to major importers of Iron Ore
like Japan and South Korea which together accounts for about 40 - 45% of sea-borne trade.
 
                      (ii)      The licenses are for limited quantity with a validity period of two/three years.  Therefore it is not possible
for NMDC to enter into an agreement/MOU on long-term basis with foreign buyers.
 
                     (iii)      NMDC has to ensure the parity of foreign exchange realization on exports on product-to-product basis with
MMTC.  Thus NMDC is deprived the freedom to adjust the prices etc. depending upon the available
inventory levels vis-à-vis the demand pattern.
 
                    (iv)      The import license imposes the restriction on NMDC to export to Japan and South Korea but for other
countries both MMTC and NMDC will be trading the same product and the brand image of the NMDC
product will never be established.
 
                      (v)      Since NMDC gets permission for Direct Export on piece-meal basis, the foreign steel mills operators have
reservations to consider NMDC as a long-term reliable supplier of iron ore.
 
                    (vi)      Since the Export Licenses are for limited quantities, NMDC cannot offer the whole product mix comprising
of both lump ore and fine ore as required by end users.
 
21.11.2            Therefore in the best interest of exports, NMDC should have complete autonomy and be permitted to
export its iron ore without any restriction of quantity, quality or geographical location.  This will enable NMDC to
operate more like any commercial organization and take business decision, which are in its best interest
 
21.11.3            NMDC is meeting the domestic demand of iron ore to an extent of 55% and the remaining 45% only is
being sold out to international market.  As per the policy of the government iron ore is to be exported through canalising
agency i.e. MMTC. MMTC finds out market to iron ore with 65% Fe content and above, whereas NMDC has got more
quantity of iron ore lying at pit head with less than 65% Fe content for which international market is available, but not
explored by NMDC.   To take care of this product NMDC is requesting Commerce Ministry to allow NMDC to direct
export to the countries other than the purchasers from MMTC i.e. Japan, Pakistan and South Korea. NMDC has already
exported directly to its foreign buyers 1.27 lakh tonnes in 1999-00, 9.65 lakh tonnes in 2000-01and  17.12 lakh tonnes in

23.1     Keeping pace with the national policy on workers’ participation in industry, NMDC has made a remarkable
breakthrough in having various fora of joint consultation and workers’ participation since the 70s and it has become an

helped in formation of a Bipartite Committee at the corporate level in which all the unions affiliated to the Federation
irrespective of their recognition by the labour machinery, affiliation to different  Central Trade Unions, participate as
one group.  This Bipartite Committee has been working very satisfactorily and all the wage settlements and other major
issues relating to job specifications, work atmosphere and other service matters are settled amicably during the
discussions in the Bipartite Committee .
 
23.4     NMDC does not have surplus manpower in any of the category as on date due to change in market scenerio i.e

25.1  Inflated mileage on Kirandul-Kottavalasa line.
 
25.1.1.Railways have been charging freight on Kirandul-Kottavalasa line (SE Railway) by inflating the distance by 30%
NMDC has been representing for the removal of the same in view of the increased traffic handled on the line. The
inflation in distance on K-K line had been continuing since 1967. Initially it was 65.2% but with the traffic volume
increasing, this was reduced to 30% in 1981. This percentage of inflation has been continuing since then. In the last
eighteen years there has been significant increase in the traffic handled on K-K line originating iron ore movement has
gone up from 56.36 lakh tonnes in 1987-88 to 145 lakh tonnes in 2000-01. In addition, the line has been handling other
traffic particularly on account of the NALCO's alumina plant near Koraput. In addition to the budgetary increase in the
freight charges over the years since 1981, Railways had been revising the classification of iron ore upwards resulting in
further increasing in the freight charges. The classification of iron ore which was 110 in 1989-90 had increased to 120 in
1994-95 and 125 in 1999-2000. For the year 2001-02, the Railway freight in respect of iron ore has been further
increased by 3% over that of the previous year with the classification remaining unchanged at 120.
 
25.1.2  The reduction in inflated mileage would help both NMDC and other domestic customers like VSP, Essar Steel,
Ispat Industries Ltd and Vikram Ispat to improve their economy in the operations.
 
25.1.3  The Sub-Committee was informed  that the Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Ltd. is linked to  Balladilla Mines of NMDC
for sourcing its iron  ore  requirements.  The  Kothavalasa-Kirandul section (  KK Line) under  Waltair Division of S.E.
Railway measures a distance of 475 kms.  Out of this distance, 118 k.m. is  on the Eastern Ghat Section and the balance
distance is in the plains  or  plateau.  This was constructed at a  cost of Rs159 Crore. and  was  opened for traffic in 
November, 1968.  In the initial stages,  Railways levied freight charges by  inflating the distance by 65.2 percent  with
stipulation  that the freight should be levied  on discontinuous  mileage basis (i.e.)  out of  475 k.m., only 35 km (i.e.)
from Kothavalala to VSP  will be charged normal freight.  Upon a further review in  1981, the percentage of  inflation
on the total distance was reduced to 30 percent  with effect from 1.6.1981. VSP is opereating from 1989 and since then
the inflated freight charge is being levied.  VSP has  transported 463.91 lakh tonnes upto March, 2002 and paid a freight
of Rs.1634.34 crore .Had VSP paid normal freight  (i.e.)  Rs.1284 crore  paid upto 2001-02 , VSP would have saved

freight  charge formed a part of the chapter on " assistance from the Government" in MOUs  signed with RINL.
 
25.1.7  In the meeting of  the Sub-Committee  held on 12
th September, 2001 on the subject of "Key Concern Areas of
Steel Industries and promotion of steel consumption in various sectors of economy ", the issue of inflated freight charge 
was  discussed in detailed.  Participating in discussion  Shri R.N. Malhotra, Chairman, Railway Board  expressed his
views :-
 
" On the questions of concessions, I would like to say that we are prepared to consider any request from any
manufacturer for certain concessions which will help them and which in turn would help the Railways.  But Sir, by
reducing our revenue, we cannot help anyone.  If they are prepared to give us  an undertaking that  if we  reduce the
freight on the KK Line by a certain percentage, they will be able to give us so much  of extra  traffic, we can consider
it."
 
25.1.8  Interjecting in the discussion, the Secretary, Ministry of Steel expressed   his opinion in following words:-
 
" The question that has been raised with regard to the KK Line related to movement of iron ore from Bailadilla,
which is used by the Vizag Steel Plant.  It has a very long history.    It is not really a question of incremental traffic.  The
operative issue here is that 65 per cent additional freight charge was put at a certain  point  of time because that line was
specifically created for the movement of iron ore from point A to point  B,  with an understanding that if the level of
freight crossed six million tonnes, this additionality would   be removed.  The  situation today is that, as against the 65
per cent  enhanced rate that was being charged, the  current enhanced rate is 30 per cent, and the traffic  generated on
that line, today,  12 tonnes. We can not have a persistent kind of an incremental situation going on.  We understand that
at a point of time, the line was constructed for captive use, and additional charges were levied in order to make it viable
for the Railways.  Once a certain threshold of traffic generation has been achieved, the incremental rate should not
apply.  That was the original understanding.  One cannot have a situation wherein because  there is an incremental rate,
in order to reduce it, you must have incremental traffic.  The fact  that rate was brought down from 65 per cent  to 35 per
cent and now to 30 per cent is, itself, a recognition of the  understanding on which this 65 per cent  was  charged.  Now,
as per that understanding, that additionally factor should now go.  This  is the issue that has to be examined.
 
25.1.9  Responding to the arguments of Secretary, the Chairman, Railway Board, added :-
 
            " The Additionally which was charged earlier was for several reasons.  The first reason was that because it was a
hilly area, with sharp edges and curves, the construction cost of rails was very high.  The second reason was that we had
put surcharge on  movement of any traffic on that line because of the fact that in place of one locomotive, which is
normally required on a  plain terrain, we had to put three locomotive in place .  So, the cost of operation also was very
high.   Also, the  electricity  bill for the  operational  of  this line is five times higher than what it would cost in the case
of   a line on the plain.  Now, how do we recover that cost ?  We cannot go on reducing our revenue, unless there is a
commitment on the part of the steel plants that they will be able to sell so much of extra steel and thus give us that much
of extra traffic.".

Para 2.5
ALLOCATION OF FUNDS
RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee noted that many of the Central PSEs are making losses due to their inability to face the competition, because of their obsolete
R&D, high cost of production, shortage of work orders, etc. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Heavy Industry should
infuse capital, state of the art technology and entrepreneurship into potentially viable PSEs so as to make these ‘Modern Temples’ capable to face the
private sector MNCs in the consumer economy.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        The strategies for strengthening and improving the potentially viable PSEs include:---
           1.    Revival of PSEs through BIFR.
           2.    Financial restructuring wherever appropriate.
           3.    Joint Venture formation to have continuous access to technology, finance and marketing.
           4.    Manpower rationalization.
        Out of 26 BIFR referred PSUs under the Department of Heavy Industry revival plans have been sanctioned by BIFR in case of 12 PSUs. These
involve cash infusion of Rs.654 crore by the Government besides financial restructuring of Rs.2106 crores. Apart from BIFR sanctioned revival
plans, Government has on its own, approved the financial restructuring in case of 7 other sick/loss making PSUs involving fresh infusion of funds to
the extent of Rs.531 crores and financial restructuring of Rs.1443 crores.
        In order to rationalize the manpower, Government have provided an amount of about Rs.1700 crores under Voluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS)
for retiring about 70,000 employees of PSUs.
        Lagan Jute Machinery Co. Ltd. (LJMC), a subsidiary of Bharat Bhari Udyog Nigam Ltd. (BBUNL) and Belting division of Andrew Yule & Co.
Ltd. have already been converted into joint venture companies. Also in case of 30 PSUs of Department of Heavy Industry, the process of JV
formation/disinvestments has been initiated.
Para 2.6
RECOMMENDATION
        In the wake of growing financial crunch in many of the Central PSEs, the Committee recommends that the Government should provide financial
assistance in the form of working capital, Non-plan loan, Government guarantee, etc. to PSEs which are potentially viable.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        Government has been providing financial assistance to the needy PSEs for the working capital (e.g. salary and wages, employees related dues
etc.) and VRS/VSS as non-plan loans. The funds released during the last three years are as follows:---

2001-2002 787.04
(Company-wise details given in Annexure-I).
        Government is also giving guarantees for raising loans from the Financial Institution for meeting their working capital requirement etc. Total
sum guaranteed by the Government for various PSEs as on March, 31,.2002 is Rs.1333.20 crore.
Para 2.9
RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee recommends that while rationalising the Government equity in non-strategic PSEs, interests of the workers should be protected
fully.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        The Government is fully alive to the need to protect the interests of the workers. Provisions in the Shareholder agreements generally incorporate
the following clauses regarding employee protection.
        1.     The parties envision that all employees of the Company on the date thereof shall continue in the employment of the Company.
        2.     The Company shall not retrench any part of its labour force for a stipulated period from the closing date other than any dismissal or
termination of employees of the Company from their employment in accordance with the standing orders/disciplinary rules of the Company.

        Funds to meet the full requirement of the six closed PSEs i.e. Mining and Allied Machinery Corporation (MAMC), Bharat Process and

Para 6.2
GUARANTEE FEE SUBSIDY
RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee is constrained to note that the Department of Heavy Industry has provided for the provision of guarantee fee subsidy to only four
PSEs in 2001-02 leaving most of the needy PSEs to face hardships in getting bank finance. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Government should provide guarantee fee subsidy to the needy PSEs for leveraging finance for sustaining their operations.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        It may be mentioned that Government has already given guarantees to number of PSEs under DHI for cash credit facilities from Banks/Financial
Institutions for meeting working capital requirements. The total sum guaranteed by the Government for various PSEs under DHI as on March 31,
2002 is Rs.1333.20 crore. The guarantee fee is only 1% of the guarantee given. The guarantee fee subsidy provided to Hindustan Cables Ltd., Burn
Standard Company Ltd. Hindustan Machine Tools Ltd. And Heavy Engineering Corporation Ltd. Mentioned in the para was as per the approved
revival schemes of these PSEs. A new scheme was also introduced in 2000-01 for providing interest subsidy on bank finance to PSEs, for
implementation of VRS. As per this scheme, 50% of the interest due on funds raised through bonds for VRS is disbursed as interest subsidy to the
PSEs concerned, which is much higher than the guarantee fee subsidy. However, guarantee fee subsidy as approved by the Government in the revival
plans of the PSEs, will continue to be provided.
Para 6.6 ---- 6.7
RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee recommends that under this new scheme introduced by DHI, more funds should be given to Richardson & Cruddas (R&C),
Tung Bhadra Steel Products Ltd. (TSPL), Triveni Structurals Ltd, Instrumentation Ltd, Burn Standard Company Ltd (BSCL) and Hindustan Cables
Ltd. (HCL). To so as to meet their demands to finance manpower rationalisation programme undertaken in these PSEs.
        The Committee further recommends that in case the amount earmarked is not sufficient for this purpose, the additional allocations may be
sought at RE stage.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        A Budget provision of Rs.10 crore was made in BE 2000-01 for interest subsidy on Bank Finance to PSEs for raising funds from
Banks/Financial Institutions for VRS in order to reduce the burden on the Companies. The initial response from the PSEs was not quite encouraging
as the scheme represented a marked departure from the prevailing practice of extending full budgetary support for VRS. Hence the provision was
reduced to Rs.1 crore at RE stage. Out of that provision of Rs.1 crore, only Rs.44.37 lakh could be utilized by one PSE viz., Richardson and Cruddas.
A budget provision per Rs. 20 crore was made in 2001-02 for this purpose. There was good response from the PSEs and a total amount of  Rs. 21.28
crore i.e. Rs. 1.28 crore more than the budget provision was released (HMT – Rs. 20.71 crore, Richardson and Cruddas – Rs. 0.25 crore and
Tungabhadra Steel Products – Rs. 0.32 crore). Consequent of this better response, the budget provision has been enhanced to Rs. 25 crore in BE
2002-03. Out of this provision an amount of Rs. 10.03 crore has already been released in the first quarter of the financial year 2002-03 to Richardson
and Cruddas (Rs. 0.25 crore), Bharat Heavy Plates and Vessels Ltd.  (Rs. 0.86 crore) and HMT (Rs. 8.92 crore). Funds will be released to the PSEs as
and when the demand is received. However, if need arises, additional funds will be sought at RE stage or by way of supplementary demands for
grants at the appropriate time.

RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee is constrained to note that keeping in view the restructuring/revival schemes going on in various PSEs, the Government has
allocated a meager amount of Rs.100.00 crores as Budgetary Support. The Committee, therefore, recommends that additional allocation, if any, may
be considered at RE stage keeping in view the requirements of the respective PSEs.

        The plan allocation of Rs. 100 crores as budgetary support to this Department would be sufficient for meeting the presently estimated
requirements of PSEs. As in the previous years, additional funds will be sought at RE stage for any additional demands due to restructuring during the
course of the year.

RECOMMENDATION
        Since a number of PSEs are running under losses, the Committee is of the view that the allocated amount of Rs.150.00 crores for revival

Committee, therefore, recommends that additional allocations, if required, may be made at the RE stage.

the demands of the PSEs, additional allocation for the purpose will be sought at RE stage through supplementary demands for grants.

ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT

RECOMMENDATION

RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee views REIL as a potentially viable PSE, which needs fresh infusion of funds so as to update its R&D and projects. The

ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        REIL, Jaipur, was incorporated on August 12, 1981 as a Joint Venture between Instrumentation Limited, Kota (ILK); a Public Sector
Undertaking (PSU), under the Department of Heavy Industry (DHI) and Rajasthan State Industrial Development and Investment Corporation
Limited, Jaipur (RIICO), with 51% to 49% ratio. Government interest in REIL is through the shareholding in REIL, as the Government holds 100%

HINDUSTAN CABLES LTD. (HCL)
RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee is happy to note that with the concerted efforts of the Government by applying restructuring plan, the Company’s decline has
stopped and its turnover increased from Rs.203.00 crores in 1999-2000 to Rs.975.00 crores in 2000-01. The Committee feels that this record turnover

RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee is constrained to note that even after the persistent efforts of the Government, the revival/restructuring package has failed in
many of the PSEs such as Mining & Allied Machinery Corporation Ltd.(MAMC), Burn Standard Co. Ltd(BSCL), Heavy Engineering Corporation
(HEC), Triveni Structural Ltd (TSL), etc. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should make a sustainable long-term revival
package in the sick but potentially viable PSEs only. The Committee also recommends that tainted sick/unviable PSEs, where revival package has not
resulted any profits, should either be privatized or closed down so as to save the already eroded public money.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        The Government’s policy towards the public sector is
        (i)    Restructure and revive potentially viable PSUs;
        (ii)    Close down PSUs which cannot be revived
        (iii)   Bring down Government equity in all non-strategic PSUs to 26% or lower if necessary and
        (iv)   Fully protect the interest of workers.
        A fresh infusion of funds of Rs. 654 crores and financial restructuring of Rs. 2106 crores have been provided by the Government in case of 12
BIFR sanctioned revival plans. Besides, Government on its own approved the financial restructuring of 7 other sick / loss making PSUs involving
fresh infusion of funds to the extent of Rs. 531 crores and financial restructuring of Rs. 1443 crores.
        The undertakings of the 7 PSUs namely Mining and Allied Machinery Corporation Ltd. (MAMC), National Bicycle India Limited(NBCIL),
Bharat Process & Mechanical Engineers Ltd. (BPMEL), Weighbird India Ltd. (WIL), Rehabilitation Industries Corporation Ltd. (RIC), Tannery and
Footwear Company Ltd. (TAFCO) and Cycle Corporation of India Ltd. (CCIL) have been closed after all the efforts for their revival have failed.
        JV/disinvestments process has been initiated in case of 30 PSUs under DHI. The list of these PSUs is given at Annexure-II.

RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee is constrained to note that despite the financial restructuring as approved by BIFR, many of the Central PSEs such as Burn &
Standard Co. Ltd., Instrumentation Ltd., Jessop & Co. Ltd. and Triveni Structurals Ltd. are still laggings far behind their targets. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that an early decision may be taken on setting up of joint ventures and/or merger of these PSEs. The Committee hopes that
after joint venture/merger, these PSEs would be able to revive themselves financially.

Co. Ltd. (BSCL), Instrumentation Ltd. Kota (ILK), Jessop & Co. Ltd. (Jessop) and Triveni Structural Ltd. (TSL).
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS
        The Committee observes that despite the financial restructuring approved by the Department of Heavy Industry and revival scheme approved by
the BIFR the marginally profit making companies/sick companies are not able to revive themselves. The causes may be cited as limited financial
resources, lack of organizational, financial skills and expertise, marketing difficulties, delayed and inadequate credit, labour problems, obsolete
technology, globalisation of economy etc. The Committee recommends that management of the PSUs who are given restructuring/revival schemes
should inform the Department of Heavy Industry when they face problems, which could lead to sickness. The progress of the Unit should be kept
under close watch of the Department of Heavy Industry and additional finance may be provided, if need be, so as to bring back the PSUs to healthy
track. The Committee further recommends that Department of Heavy Industry should also help the PSUs in sorting out difficulties which are non-
financial in nature and require assistance from outside agencies like Government departments./Undertakings/Electricity Boards etc.
Para 9.18-9.21
BHARAT HEAVY ELECTRICALS LIMITED (BHEL)
RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee, in the first instance, regrets to note that even though the Conference of Chief Ministers had resolved to set up an Expert Group
to recommend one time settlement of all power sector outstanding dues to Central PSEs and dues from Central PSEs to State Power Utilities, the
Ahluwalia Committee restricted the scope of their study to one time settlement of dues relating to electricity and fuel supplied to SEBs by Central
PSEs excluding Central PSEs like BHEL, PFC etc. as their dues were on the capital account.
        The Committee noted that pursuant to its recommendations and efforts made by DHI, the Ministry of Power had proposed to include the
outstanding dues of BHEL and AYCL also in the scheme worked out by the Ahluwalia Committee. The Committee, however, is disappointed to note
that Government has not accepted the proposal of the Ministry of Power, and has excluded BHEL/AYCL from the scheme, presumably on account of
the fact that the Ahluwalia Committee had recommended one time settlement of SEBs’ dues in respect of only those Central PSEs which are
supplying electricity and fuel to the SEBs.
        The Committee would like to place on record its appreciation of the role played by BHEL and other Central PSEs like Andrew Yule Co. Ltd.
(AYCL) over the last 40 years for development and growth of the power sector. The health of equipment supplying Central PSEs (BHEL, AYCL
etc.) is an important for the power sector as that for Central PSEs supplying electricity and fuel. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends to
the Government to review its decision and include BHEL and AYCL in the one time settlement scheme for outstanding dues.
        The Committee also recommends that if issue of liquidation of the outstanding dues of BHEL is not resolved, then, it may be placed before the
Cabinet Committee.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs did not agree to the proposal of Ministry of Power to include BHEL’s case for one time settlement
of SEBs alongwith other PSUs. The Department of Heavy Industry is considering the matter regarding liquidation of outstanding dues of BHEL
independent of the Ahluwalia Committee recommendations.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee notes that Department of Heavy Industry is considering the matter regarding liquidation of outstanding dues of Bharat Heavy
Electrical Ltd. Independent of the Ahluwalia Committee recommendations. The Committee recommends that Department of Heavy Industry should
also consider case of Andrew Yule Co. Ltd. For liquidation of its outstanding SEB dues.

coordinate implementation of the Auto Policy, steer resolution of Inter-Ministerial issues and to remove impediments which hinder desired growth of

Para 9.8 – 9.10
PRICE PREFERENCE TO DOMESTIC INDUSTRY
RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee is concerned to note that the domestic manufacturers are not able to avail price preference of 15% for projects funded by
international agencies like World Bank, United Nations, Asian Development Bank etc. as imports on such projects is allowed at ‘nil’ duty as per
Notification No.85/99-customs dated July 6, 1999. The power projects for 10th and 11th Five Year Plans are being finalised. Some of these projects
may entail multilateral funding. Additional power projects of 60,000 MW during the 11 th plan period are likely to be finalised. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the Customs Notification No. 85/99 – custom dated July 6, 1999 should be rescinded to enable domestic manufacturers to
effectively compete against foreign suppliers by taking advantage of 15% price preference provided in ICB tenders.
        The Committee views this issue very seriously since it has effected zero customs duty regime applicable to all goods imported to India for
execution of projects financed by the United Nations/World Bank or any other International Organisation. This amended custom duty structure has
adversely affected competitiveness of the domestic Capital Goods industries.
        The Committee, therefore, recommends that this anomaly needs to be rectified at the earliest possible. The Committee also recommends that if
need arises then the DHI should take up this issue with the Ministry of Finance (Department of Revenue) to resolve the log jam. The Committee
further recommends that the unresolved matter may be placed before the Cabinet Committee to consider the matter de-novo.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        This matter has been discussed in the Department related Parliamentary Standing Committee. They had constituted a separate Committee headed
by Revenue Secretary for making recommendations on this issue. They have since given their recommendations stating that World Bank guidelines
provide for giving preferential treatment to domestic bidders. Their recommendations were discussed in a meeting on 12.08.2002 by the Standing
Committee (Sub-Committee-III). Further action on these recommendations of the Parliamentary Standing Committee for issue of clarifications is
being taken by the Department of Revenue.
Para 9.11
REFUND OF TERMINAL EXCISE DUTY TO DOMESTIC INDUSTRIES
RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee is concerned to note that the domestic manufacturers continue to suffer cost disadvantages such as sales tax, octroi, and high cost
of finance and infrastructure bottlenecks to the extent of 18-28% while competing with imports. At present custom duty on Coal Mining, Fertilizer
and Power projects is 5% basic custom duty+16% CVD and ‘nil’ SAD. Under this structure the domestic industry is unable to claim refund of excise
duty and become uncompetitive. The Committee, therefore, recommends that there should be no duty free import of projects and a minimum of 15%
basic custom duty + ‘nil’ CVD + 4% SAD be imposed to enable the domestic industry to become competitive without increasing the project cost.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        The issue has already been taken up by DHI with Ministry of Finance vide D.O. letter No. 3(23)/99-PE.XI dated December 29,.2000. Hon’ble
Minister (HI & PE) vide D.O. letter dated December 23, 2000 has also taken up various issues including the above with Hon’ble Finance Minister
(copy enclosed) (Annexure-VII).

Companies are unable to absorb the 16% excise duty which is quite substantial. This has been affecting adversely the functioning of all power
companies and particularly the BHEL. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Government/DGFT should make a special measure
for refund of Terminal Excise Duty for those projects/bids, which were finalized (under International Competitive Bidding) before March 31, 2000
for maintaining the continuity of the existing EXIM Policy for projects/bids affected.

Committee-III. DGFT have informed this Department that they are not in favour of extending the benefit of refund of Terminal Excise Duty if the
supplies have been effected on or after April 1, 2000, even if LOI had been opened prior to March 31, 2000. Further they have stated that the matter is
sub judice.

        The Committee recommends that while rationalizing the duty structure compatible with WTO guidelines, the Government should protect the
interests of the domestic paper industries.
        The Committee views the Government’s Policy of reducing customs duty from 35% to 30% as against the WTO bound rate of 40% as a major
threat for the domestic paper industries. The Committee conceives that the reduction in customs duty would definitely encourage import, which in
turn, would adversely affect the paper industries. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should review its decision and revise
the custom duty to 35% or 40%.

industries. The Committee also recommends that the BHI should take up this subject with the Ministry of Finance (Department of Revenue) for
reversing the custom duty on newsprint from the present 5% to 20% which is still lower to the WTO bond rate of 25%.

Dear Shri Yashwant Sinhaji,
        As you are aware the capital goods industry is witnessing an unprecedented demand recession, causing declining market prices and erosion in
domestic market share. Capital goods sector has witnessed a decline of 2.7% in April-Sept.2000 as compared to a growth of 5% in 1999-2000 and
11% in 1998-99.
2.     Some of the factors responsible for deceleration are slow down in investment, reduction in the custom duty on capital goods/project imports
from a high of 85% to 0-5%. Domestic manufacturers continue to suffer cost disadvantages such as sales tax, octroi, high cost of finance and

101st report of Committee on Industry

infrastructure bottlenecks to the extent of 18-28% while competing with imports.
3.     This situation is further aggravated by the issue of notification No.85/99 dated 6.7.99 which allows import of goods for the projects financed by
the United Nations, World Bank, Asian Development Bank and other International organizations at “Nil” duty. Due to this notification, domestic
manufacturers are not able to avail the price preference of 15% for projects funded by such agencies.
4.     You are aware that the capital goods sector has very strong backward and forward linkages. Therefore, it is necessary to provide support to give
the desired impetus to this industry for reversing the declining trend and sustain its growth. In this context, I have following suggestions for your
consideration -----
        l     Custom Duty on all capital goods should be brought to bound rate of WTO.
        l     In project imports, restructure this present duty structure by levying minimum basic custom duty of 15% + CVD equal to excise duty @ 8%
or lower and rescind notification No.85/99 dated 6.7.99.
        l     Restoration of Terminal Excise Duty (TED) to domestic suppliers to projects where the end product is not exciseable.
        With regards,

CHAPTER–I
MEMORANDUM  OF  UNDERSTANDING  BETWEEN  FERTILIZER  PSUS  AND DEPARTMENT  OF 
FERTILIZERS
1.1       The commitments and mutual responsibilities of the Government and the PSUs are clearly defined in the MoU
System. The targets are finalised at the beginning of the year and so are the commitments of the Department of
Fertilizers. The evaluation of the performance of these targets is carried out only at the end of the year. The focus under
the MoU system hence is said to have shifted from mere input orientation to result orientation. This also envisages a
system granting more autonomy to the PSUs with lesser involvement of the Ministries and Departments in the control of
the day-to-day functioning of the PSUs through laid down procedures etc.

2.1       MFL was incorporated in December, 1966 as a public sector undertaking with authorised share capital of Rs. 14
crores in December, 1966 with Government of India and AMOCO India Inc. (a wholly owned subsidiary of Standard
Oil Company of USA) holding 51% and 49% shares respectively. MFL commenced commercial production in
November, 1971. Subsequently, in 1972 as per the Formation Agreement, National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC - a
multi billion state-owned petro-chemical company of Iran) was inducted as shareholder acquiring 50% of AMOCO
shareholding in MFL.
2.2       In 1985, AMOCO, pursuant to their worldwide strategy, disinvested their shares, which were in turn acquired by
Government of India and NIOC. The current shareholding pattern is as follows :
            Government of India                                                     58.74%

            Public                                                                           15.82%
            The paid-up equity capital of the company as on 31.3.2000 is Rs. 162.05 crores.
2.3       MFL is engaged in the manufacture of Ammonia, Urea, complex fertilizers and bio-fertilizers. MFL's activities
include marketing of these fertilizers and trading in Agro-chemicals in accordance with the corporate objective. MFL
has its plant facilities and head quarters located on a sprawling 350 acres at Manali, about 20 kms. north of Chennai

CAPTIVE  POWER
2.7       MFL consumes around 130 million unit of electrical power per year drawn from TNEB grid and also from
captive generation. 8 Diesel Generators and 2 Gas Turbines generate 32.7 million units (25%) per year as captive power.
2.8       To tide over frequent power failure, under-frequency and voltage fluctuations of TNEB grid, MFL is seeking
alternate power capacity from outside supply sources other than TNEB.
2.9       MFL had preliminary discussion with Chennai Petroleum Corporation Limited (CPCL) for participation in their
proposed Rs. 2837 crore Independent Power Plant (IPP) Project of 500 MW capacity.
2.10     In the meantime, MFL is holding negotiation with CPCL for wheeling 4 to 5 MW of surplus power from their
existing captive Power Plant facility.
2.11     The company did not pay dividend to its shareholders after 1992-93. It is running in losses. The loss was
contributed by shortfall in production of urea and NPK, reduction in contribution for NPK, higher specific consumption
of raw materials, steep exchange rate variation, monsoon failure resulting in lower sales, higher rebates and discounts
and higher interest cost.
2.12     The company's operations continue to be unprofitable. During April and May 2001, Ammonia plant load had to
be restricted due to high Ammonia inventory levels caused by poor off-take by downstream urea/NPL plants. Similarly,
urea plant was also operated at low levels as off-take of NPK for sale has been poor. The annual turnaround was taken
up on May 28, 2001 with a schedule to complete it on June 22, 2001. However, due to the unexpected developments,
the turnaround was extended and the company could come back to production stream in respect of NH
3 only on August
3, 2001. Keeping in view the advice given by urea reactor manufacturers, the company decided to get the urea reactor
inspected which was not envisaged in the original schedule. The inspection of reactor was a difficult job involving
erection of structure above the reactor with hoisting facility. Though an attempt was made to erect the structure while
the plant was in operation, enough progress could not be made due to unfavourable environmental conditions. After the
shut down of the plants, erection work was taken up and hoists were provided at the top level of about 60 mtrs. height to
life the reactor bundles, each weighing 36 T. Reactor B was inspected on July 18 and after attending to some minor
repairs was boxed up.
2.13     In contrast, the inspection of reactor 'A' revealed extensive damages. A quick assessment was made and
necessary action was initiated by the company to rectify the bundles. Notwithstanding all these constraints, the company
decided to start and run the Ammonia and Urea plants at around 50% load. The quality of Urea being produced now is
relatively better with temperature of the Prill hovering around 50
o Celsius, which are the main objectives of Urea Prill
Tower modifications, aimed and achieved by the company. The repair works to Reactor 'A' involve procurement of
imported materials, extensive welding and other specialized jobs, which has been entrusted on a turnkey basis to the
manufacturer M/s Nooter Fabricators Inc. USA to secure Guarantee Test Run of urea plant.

formulate an Auto Policy in view of the ongoing liberalization of the economy and W.T.O. obligations. In response to

actions by the Ministries other than the Department of Heavy Industries and so far these recommendations had not been
translated into real Government Policy.

the meeting held on 16th July, 2002 the Committee had interacted with Automotive Research Association of India
(ARAI); Society of India Automobiles Manufacturers (SIAM); Automotive Tyre Manufacturers Association (ATMA)
and Automotive Component Manufacturers Association (ACMA); Prozon Inc. (manufacture of fuel saver). Apprising

Recommendation (Para 1.3)
COMMON MISSION FOR ACHIEVING COMMON ORGANIZATIONAL GOAL

The Committee notes the stages involved in the formation of Bharat Refractories Ltd.
(BRL) and hopes that BRL management would leave no storie untumed in assessing the strength
ofall the four units of BRL and chalk out a short and long term strategic course of action for early
turnaround of Company as a whole. The Committee recommends that BRL management work to
ensure that all four units of BRL are making effort towards the common mission for achieving
common organizational goal and are contributing to the physical and financial performance of the

' Company. None of them must prove a burden on the Company.

Action Taken

A Techno-Economic Viability study of BRL was conducted by MECON Limited. This
study provides a complete road map for BRL to Teorganize its activities and revive its financial
and physical performance. Based on this study the Company proposed a revival package which
Was approved, by the Government in June, 2002. Following this approval, the Company and the
Government have taken steps to implement the revival plan in a time bound manner. It is
anticipated that the positive impact of this revival plan, based on the above mentioned study,
would start to become evident from January, 2003 onwards.

Recommendation (Para 2.5)

CAPITAL STRUCTURE

The Committee is constrained to exits its concern over the deteriorating balance sheet
of BRL. The Committee in its 34" and 50% Report has been recommending to the Government
to provide sufficient working capital to BRL at the earliest so that it could reduce its losses, loans
and liability and readjust itself for profit making track. The Committee, in this regard,
recommends that the BRL management and the Ministry of Steel should examine and assess the
capital structure of BRL, from time, to time and Suggest measures for capital restructuring, in
such a way that BRL achieves the break even point and economy of scales ensuring maximum
Retum on Investment (ROI).

Action Taken

The Government of India has already approved a revival package for BRL based on a
Techno-Economic Viability study conducted by MECON Limited. This package provides for
Government of India loans, on soft terms for implementing a new VR Scheme and for liquidating
liabilities towards unpaid statutory dues, wages and salaries to all employees availing of VRS.
Additionally the Government of India has agreed to provide a Government of India Guarantee to
enable the Company to raise Rs.30 crores for its working capital requirements. As part of capital
restructuring the Government of India has converted its existing loans to the extent of Rs. 97.89



ee into equity. The Government of India has also provided equity of Rs, 7 crore each y
5 years to enable the Company to undertake AMR Jobs. With these measures It is hoped that the

Company would be able to improve its balance sheet and achieve break even point within the
next 2 to 3 years.

Recommendation (Para 9.2 )

POSITION OF INVENTORIES.

It is but natural that a Company which lacks sufficient working capital and there is a low
demand of its products would have little inventories, and Bharat Refractories Ltd. is no exception
to this rule, the Committee observes. However, the Committee feels that the BRL management
should keep a constant watch on the inventories and dispose of the inventory as and when the
same accumulates because even small inventory, since the volume of production is confined to
the availability of capital and market demand, would further block the scarce resources of
working capital and thereby creating ‘Vicious - circle’ of insufficient working capital, high low
production and no inventories. Sufficient working capital, high volume of production and low
inventory should be the motto of the Company,

Imbalance between manufacturing cost and selling price
Recommendation (Para 7.9 )

The Committee understands the problems being faced by Refractories industry erising
due to imbalance between manufacturing cost and selling price. The Committee observe that the
Price of the finished Products has been drastically reduced (ranging from 30 to 44 एल cent)
whereas there is a trend in increase in the Price structure of input materials
(ranging from 5 to 17 per cent). This is the double loss to the refractory industry and under the
said circumstances any industry is bound to be affected, Therefore, the Committee is of the view
that refractories industry in general and BRL management in particular should chalk out a two
pronged strategy ie. one to arrest the fall in the selling price of refractories and to reverse the
tend and other strategy is required to minimize the cost of Production so that the margin of profit
for refractories industry may increase. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry of
Steel should act as a facilitator and guide the BRL management to undertake measures for
maximization of profit,

contained in  the  Committee ' s  85
th Report  on Implementation Status of Financial  Assistance-cum-restructuring

Recommendations/Observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry of Steel  
 
(Chapter - I).
Recommendations:- 2.2 ,  3.2,  4.2 , 4.8, 5.2, 5.4, 5.10,  and  6.4 ,

3.         The Committee is pleased to observe that  the   Ministry of Steel has accepted its  recommendations  as 
mentioned in Chapter –I of the  Report. 
4.                  In respect of the recommendation made in Para 4.4  in Chapter-II  the Committee is  convinced  with the logic
and explanation  advocated by the Ministry of  Steel  and therefore   does not want to  pursue  further .
5.         The Committee expresses its concern over the non-implementations  of recommendations contained in  Chapter-
III  and therefore  the Committee desires that the Ministry of Steel should furnish  logical  explanation  in respect of
these recommendations.
6.         In respect  of recommendations placed in Chapter-IV, the Ministry of Steel has  either   furnished the interim
replies or couched its language in  vague terms like  noted for compliance/guidance therefore, the Committee desires 
that the Ministry of Steel would furnish Action Taken Notes in  respects of recommendation categorized   in Chapter-
IV  in detail and to the point, as per the intention and spirit of the recommendations of the Committee.
7.         Observations/recommendations of the Committee  are given in Chapter (V)
8.         The Details of the Action Taken Notes is being discussed in various Chapters in the succeeding pages.
 
 
CHAPTER - I
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
 
           
Recommendation (Para 2.2 )
 
Financial Performance of HSCL
 
            The Committee, while taking note of the current financial performance of HSCL expresses its concern
over its pathetic condition, and is of the view that HSCL needs improvement for better financial performance. 
HSCL requires a new vision, new managerial will and effective strategy for the continuance of its existence.
           
Action Taken
 
The Ministry of Steel has noted the observation of the Committee.  The financial performance of the Company
improved during 2001-02 over the previous Financial Year  2000-2001.  Major parameters are indicated below:
(Rs. in crore)
FACTORS 2000-01 2001-02 IMPROVEMENT
Turnover 242.95 257.89 14.94 (6%)
Gross Margin (PBIDT)  (-) 117.32 (-) 58.74 58.58 (50%)
Net Margin (-) 127.69* (-) 72.89* 54.80 (43%)
Salary & Wages 105.72 73.66 32.06 (30%)
* Excluding terminal benefits
            .
This improvement is continuing  during the present Financial Year 2002-03 also.  The Company has engaged the
services of a consultant to prepare a strategic plan for its further operation and management.
 
Recommendation (Para 3.2)
 
Revival Package to HSCL
 
            The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the Government for approving the financial restructuring
proposal.  Considering the fact that resources are limited the sanctioning of revival package having financial implication
is a considered decision of the Government.  Committee also appreciates the Ministry of Steel for its consistent efforts
in persuading the Ministry of Finance for giving revival package to HSCL.  The Committee notes the provisions of

104th Report of Committee on Industry

revival package for HSCL.
 
Action Taken
 
            The comment/observation of the Committee is noted.
 
Recommendation (Para 4.2. )
 
Implementation of   the provision of  revival package
 
            The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry of Steel has taken action on all provisions contained in the
revival package.  The Committee hopes that efforts of the Ministry of Steel in persuading the Department of Revenue
for exempting of corporate tax for HSCL would have a positive impact on the financial performance of HSCL.  The
Committee further hopes that consequent upon the separation of 7,106 employees and reduction in the wage bill, the
financial ratio of the Company would further improve.
 
Action Taken
 
Consequent upon separation of 7373 employees during 2000-01 & 2001-02, expenditure towards Salary &
wages  has come down by Rs. 32.06 crore in 2001-02 over 2000-01. Further reduction in cost towards wages and
salaries is expected after implementation of a fresh VRS package.
 
            Exemption from payment of Corporate Tax in 1999-2000 is within the provision of Restructuring Package.  No
demand from Income Tax Department for payment of Corporate Tax has been received.
 
Recommendation (Para 4.8:)
 
Savings on the Specified Overheads
 
            The Committee is happy to note the savings on the specified overheads due to measures undertaken by HSCL
management to rationalise administrative expenditure.  The Committee hopes that the efforts to rationalise
administrative expenditure would continue.
 
Action Taken
 
All actions are being taken to reduce administrative expenditure.  During Financial Year 2001-02,
Administrative expenditure was reduced by Rs.17 crore over the previous Financial Year  2000-01.
 
Recommendation (Para 5.2) 
 
Financial Assistance-cum-restructuring package
 
            The Committee observes that financial assistance-cum-restructuring package as proposed by the Ministry of
Steel and so approved by the Government was not as comprehensive so as to mitigate the accumulated loss and total
liability of HSCL.  The Company continues to rein in adverse financial scenario and disadvantages in general because
implementation of the revival package would respond only if approved measures are taken in time for total and
comprehensive restructuring of the Company.  HSCL needs total overhauling and complete and comprehensive
restructuring in one go as partial package and delayed implementation defeats the whole idea, approach and action.
 
Action Taken
 
Subsequent to the Financial Restructuring Package, granted by Government of India during July, 99, a proposal
for further revival of the Company was submitted in June, 01 to the Finance Ministry by Ministry of Steel.
 

104th Report of Committee on Industry

Details of the proposal are as under:-
 
1.                  Grant of non-plan assistance for settlement of outstanding salaries and other statutory liabilities amounting to
Rs.182.28 crore.
2.                  Increase the existing Government of India guarantee by Rs.250 crore to facilitate further loan from commercial
banks for separation of another 5000 employees.
 
The Ministry of Finance has sanctioned Rs. 89.44 crore towards outstanding salaries and other statutory
liabilities of separated employees.  The balance liability stands at Rs. 133 crore as on August 1,.2002.  Ministry
of Steel is examining the objections of Finance Ministry with regard to pay revision in the Company which is
coming in the way of Finance Ministry releasing adequate financial assistance to clear all dues towards
wages/salaries.
 
            Out of the required Rs.250 crore for VRS Rs.50 has already been drawn from Indian Overseas Bank  in
July, 2002.  Another Rs.50 crore has been sanctioned by Canara Bank.  Efforts are on to ensure that the entire
Rs.250 crore is raised for effecting VRS of 5000 employees.
 
            The Company has also engaged a consultant for preparing a strategic plan and a plan for organisational
restructuring.
 
Recommendation  (Para 5.4)
 
Sufficient resilience and synergy to work
 
The Committee is of the view that once the comprehensive restructuring package is effectively implemented
HSCL would acquire sufficient resilience and synergy to work even against fierce competition.  The Committee
recommends that HSCL management should strive in this regard.
 
Action Taken
 
HSCL Management has already renewed its thrust on the impending changes in strategies of Execution,
Marketing, Financial operation and all round development.  New areas of operation, such as, Power, Roads and Bridges,
Railway projects and repair, Airport development, Residential and Commercial Buildings etc. have been identified to
compensate for the decline in steel sector.  All the units will be made to function as separate profit centres for their
existence.  HRD will be a high thrust area.  Action is already on for computerization of project monitoring system at a
faster pace.  In addition as stated above a strategic plan and a plan for organisational restructuring is being prepared.
 
Recommendation ( Para 5.10)
 
Rationalisation  of  expenditure toward contract payment.
 
            The Committee is of the view that the HSCL management should have undertaken necessary steps to
rationalize expenditure toward contract payment.
 
Action Taken
 
            HSCL Management is taking all steps to reduce expenditure towards contract payment.  This is evident from the
fact that direct expenditure during 2001-02 has reduced to 82% from 92% in 2000-01.
 
Recommendation (Para 6.4) :
 
Delay  by Commercial bank in the sanction and disbursement of the first phase of loan to HSCL
 
The Committee is perturbed to note the delay of about eleven months by Commercial bank in the sanction and

104th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/104threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:24:57]
disbursement of the first phase of loan to HSCL to the tune of Rs. 210  crore for VRS purpose on the plea of adverse
financial fundamentals of HSCL.  The delay in sanctioning of loan of HSCL have rather adversely affected the so called
financial fundamental  of HSCL during that span of eleven moths in the form of payment of wage and salaries given to
HSCL employees during the span of eleventh months.  The Committee opines that idle wages and salaries given to
HSCL employees during said eleven months is a criminal wastage of money so far as the financial state of the Company
is concerned and the matter needs to be inquired into.
 
Action Taken
 
Reasons for delay in sanction of 1 st phase loan by SBI have already been explained.  HSCL Management has
tried to compensate for the delay by stepping up the VRS process.  Against the directive of separating 6000 employees
in three years, 7373 employees were separated in one and a  half years.  The Company is being asked to ensure that
there is no unreasonable delay in future.
CHAPTER –II
 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE
 
Recommendation (Para 4.4)
 
Accumulated loss of the Company
 
            The Committee understands that it is but natural that the accumulated loss of the Company would come down
once the Government grants waiver of interest Government loans, so far the same is a book-entry and it hardly has any
reflection on the actual financial performance of the Company.
 
Action Taken
 
The comment/observation of the Committee is noted.
 
CHAPTER-III
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH THE COMMITTEE HAS NOT
ACCEPTED REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY OF STEEL.
                                   
Recommendation (Para 5.6 )
Failure of financial and  revival package
 
            The Committee is constrained to express its concern over the fact that financial assistance given for restructuring
package could not be implemented in the expected manner and the outcome thereof is not as expected.  The Committee
notes the reasons for failure of revival package, although it is not fully envisaged with the reasons for failure of revival
package as advocated by the Ministry of Steel.  For the revival of the Company HSCL management has to procure work
order despite ups and downs in steel industry and HSCL management should not face much difficulties as Government
is giving due importance to the construction sector.  The Committee is of the view that optimum utilisation of
manpower and resources at the disposal of Company is the responsibility of HSCL management.
      
Action Taken
 
Despite continued decline in steel industry, HSCL secured orders worth Rs.242 crore during 2001-02 as
compared to Rs.201 crore during 2000-01.  The target for 2002-03 has been set at Rs.300 crore.
 
            HSCL Management has already taken suitable actions to ensure that the physical performance of the Company
does not slide due to drastic reduction in manpower.  This is clearly evident from the fact that the Turnover increased

from Rs.243 crore in 2000-01 to Rs.258 crore in 2001-02.  However, effort is on to optimize utilisation of resources by
way of increase  in Turnover and Order booking.
 
Further Recommendation
 
            The Committee is of the view that since the Government is giving impetus to the construction sector and because

Recommendation ( Para 7.3)
 
System of Sub-Contracting Business Pattern

work done by the Company itself.  The Committee is of the view that VRS offer by HSCL to its employees would take

REPORT
 
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Mines (Ministry of Coal and
Mines) on the Recommendations contained in the  64
th  Report (of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Industry) on  Modernisation, Restructuring  and Expansion Programme of Hindustan Zinc Ltd. (HZL) 
and  post disinvestment performance of  Hindustan  Zinc Ltd in the background of the shareholders agreement.  
Hindustan Zinc Limited (HZL),  one of the leading producers of lead and zinc, was incorporated   in January 1968 as a
public sector Company after the take over of the erstwhile Metal Corporation of India Limited, to develop mining and
smelting capacities to meet the domestic demand of zinc and lead metals..   The authotrised share capital of HZL is Rs.
500 crore and the paid up capital is Rs. 422.53 crore.  The Government held 75.92% of the equity as 24.08% of its
equity was disinvested during the period 1991-93.  Government decided to further disinvest 26% equity capital of HZL
to a strategic partner with an appropriate role in management. On 11
th April,,2002, the Government has disinvested 26%
equity of HZL and management of the company wastransferred to the Strategic Partner  (S.P.) namely, M/s Sterlite
Opportunities and Ventures Ltd. with this  disinvestment the stake  of the Government in the Company has come
down    to 49.92% . Sub-Committee   on Ministry of Mines and Coal under the  convertion of Shri A.C Jose  (LS)

CHAPTER – V
OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
1.            Management of Company Affairs
 
            The Committee notes the composition of the Board of  Directors of the Company which is expected to manage
the affairs of the company in accordance with the Articles of Association of the Company and The Companies Act
1956.  the Committee expects that new managements would ensure that no deviation is made in this regard.
 
2.         Special consent required from the Government
 
            The Committee notes the provisions identified in Schedule 4.5 of Shareholders Agreement (SHA) where special
consent is required from the Government for transecting the business pertaining of those items. The Committee
recommends that “Government Nominee Director” would actively participate in the meeting of Board of Director of the
Company and would keep the Government well informed the decision reached in the meeting.   The Governments
Nominee Director need to be vigilant and epitome of ensuring responsive and responsible management of affairs in the
Company.
 
3.            Adequate job opportunities for SC/ST physically handicapped persons
