8.1       Minerals are broadly categorized as fuel minerals, atomic minerals, metallic minerals and non-metallic minerals. Among metallic minerals,
iron and associated minerals are called ferrous minerals (iron, manganese, chrome). All non-fuel, non-atomic and other than ferrous minerals are thus
included in the scope and ambit of non-ferrous minerals (eg.bauxite, copper, gold, zinc etc. metallic minerals as well as limestone, diamond etc.
nonmetallic minerals), for which the Ministry of Mines is primarily responsible. Prior to the formulation of the Statement of Industrial Policy, 1991,
mining of iron ore, manganese ore, chrome ore, gypsum, sulphur, gold and diamond, copper, lead, zinc, tin, molybdenum and wolfram were reserved
for the public sector. Since 1991, the non-ferrous mining and metallurgical industries are mostly in the private sector, for which no direct budgetary
support is needed. The Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) under the administrative control of the Ministry of Mines in the non-ferrous mining and
metallurgical sectors are provided budgetary support to the extent necessary. Of the PSUs, only the loss making PSUs, viz. Hindustan Copper
Limited (HCL) and Bharat Gold Mines Limited (BGML) would require budgetary support during 2003-04 primarily for separating the manpower,
for which budgetary grants have been proposed. Apart from this, for extending support to the mining sector, the Ministry of Mines has proposed

budgetary support to the Geological Survey of India (GSI), and Promotional Exploration funds for  Mineral Exploration Corporation of India
(MECL), who undertake survey and exploration for minerals and to the Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM), who takes measures for regulation and
conservation of minerals. The budgetary support to GSI, MECL and IBM are expected to contribute to identification of new minerals reserves, help
in scientific mining and contribute towards overall development of the non-ferrous mining sector. 
8.2       The Committee understands that with the liberalization process in the economy the non-ferrous mining and metallurgical industries are in
private sector where no budgetary support is required and only the loss making mines PSUs i.e. HCL and BGML require budgetary support in the
forum of grants –in –aid for sepration of manpower.  Right sizing of manpower has become the order of the corporate governance in order to cut the
labour cost.  The Committee is in agreement with the Ministry of Mines for the budgetary support to the Geological Survey of India and Promotional
Exploration Funds for Mineral Exploration Co-operation Limited (MECL), which undertake survey and actions, and exploration for minerals and to
the Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM) which takes measures for regulation and conservation of minerals. However, the Committee strongly believes that 
the budgetary support  provided to GSI, MECL and IBM would contribute to identification of new minerals reserves, help in scientific mining and
contribute towards overall development of the non-ferrous mining sector. 
 
8.3       The Ministry of Mines apprised the Committee that  the Central Government has laid down the broad policy governing the mining sector,
while  the State Governments as owners of minerals grant the mineral concessions for all minerals, including the non-ferrous minerals, within the
framework laid down by the Central Government. The Ministry of Mines has constituted Mineral Advisory Council under the Chairmanship of the
Minister in Charge, in which the State Governments, the Mining and Metallurgical Industry and all other stakeholders are invited. This Council is the
Apex think tank and advises the Government towards desired policy changes for problem solving, and it is the endeavour of the Ministry to hold
meetings of the Council every year. The 27 th meeting of the Mineral Advisory Council was held on 21 st Sept., 2002. From time to time, meetings
with the investors are also held.      As a result of the interaction meetings, changes in the mining statutes have been brought about, inter-departmental
discussions for solving overlapping areas of concern have been held, and State Governments have been sensitized about local level problems of the
investors in the mining sector for corrective action.
 
8.4       The Committee is of the view that the Mineral Advisory Council should meet  at least four times in a year to sort out the problems being
faced by Mining Industry and suggest possible solutions and if required modification in the existing legal framework.  The Committee feels that
interaction of the representatives of Central Government, State Governments and investors in Mining Sector would solve the mutual problems and
thus the consensus-ad-idem and common efforts so evolved would lead to rapid growth and development of Mining Industry in general.
 
8.5       During the course of interaction with the representatives of Federation of Indian Mineral Industries (FIMI) the Committee  was apprised that
while the Government of India has liberalised the policies i.e. planned around the objective of making de-regulation and liberalization of mineral
production and processing industry a ground reality, however, the process of liberalization and dismantling regulatory regimes are yet to percolate to
the State level and to other implementing agencies. 
 
8.6       The Committee feels it imperative that policies that emanate from the Central Government should percolate to the State Government as well
as the implementing agencies in the spirit in which these policies are pronounced.  It is expected that the Mineral Advisory Council in its meeting
should persuade the representative of the State Government as well as the implementing agencies to bring out the necessary amendments in the
existing laws, rules and regulations to harmonize  the policy and practice.
 
8.7       In reply to the Committee’s query as to what extent the private enterprises has entered into non-ferrous Mining and Metallurgical Industries
and the steps  being taken to promote foreign investment, the Ministry of Mines replied that according to the information maintained by the Indian
Bureau of Mines (IBM), about 90% of the total mining leases in the country are held in the private sector, comprising about 65% of the total area
granted under mining lease. The National  Mineral Policy, 1993 promoted induction of private investment including foreign investment in the mining
sector, including in the non-ferrous mining sector. The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 (MMDR Act) was amended in
1994 and 1999. The Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 (MCR) and the Mineral Conservation and Development Rules, 1988 (MCDR), framed under
the MMDR Act, 1957 have also been  modified.
 
8.8       In so far as the policy regarding foreign direct investment (FDI) is concerned, in 1994, the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation)
Act, 1957 was amended to remove bottlenecks to induction of foreign equity for mining proposals. While FDI was normally limited to 50% this
limitation did not apply to captive mines of any minerals processing industry, and enhanced equity holdings could also be considered on case to case
basis. In 1997, this policy was further fine-tuned to allow induction of FDI up to 50% on an automatic basis. Since February 2000, all proposals for
foreign direct investment in the mining sector are eligible for automatic approval, subject to ceilings on foreign equity on the mineral concerned for
such approval. Except for precious stones and diamonds, automatic approval of foreign direct investment up to 100% is permissible for gold, silver
and all other non fuel and non atomic minerals. For precious stones and diamonds, automatic approval for foreign direct investment is permissible up
to 74%. Till 31st January 2002, the total number of foreign direct investment proposals approved through the Foreign Investment Promotion Board
(FIPB) with most of the leading global mining companies evincing interest in India was 72, indicating an expected FDI inflow of Rs.4018 crore.   In
October 1996, the Ministry of Mines had issued guidelines to facilitate large area aerial prospecting, in response to which, the entrepreneurs have
taken 65 large area prospecting licenses, covering an area of over 90 thousand square kilometers. After the amendment in the MMDR Act, 1957 in
1999, 119 reconnaissance permits covering an area of over 1,55,000 (approx.) thousand square kilometers have been granted.
 
8.9       The Committee understands that    since the  adoption of the policy of liberalization and  privatization    Government is  withdrawing from
commercial ventures, and  therefore, the proportionate   increase in the participation of private sector in the transaction of business /commercial
venture is but natural .  The Committee   is in agreement with the view of Ministry of Mines that the promulgation of  new National Mineral Policy in
1993  has opened   the gate for  private player into non-ferrous mining and metallurgical   industries.  However, the Committee is of the view that   it
is the time to review the extent of participation of private sector  into the mining sector.  The Committee recommends that   a review panel should be
constituted  to examine the following issues  and the findings of the   panel  be furnished to this Committee for  forming   its final  opinion:-
(i.) to examine the comprehensiveness of National Mineral Policy, 1993 and suggest amendments if required.

9.3.13  The Committee is of the opinion that the Planning Commission and the Ministry of Finance after considering the financial health of MECL
should give due consideration to the financial restructuring programmes of MECL instead of evaluating  the confidence level of MECL and its self
sustaining resilience.  On the one hand a rider i.e. separation of 500 more employees is put up for sanctioning the comprehensive and financial
restructuring proposals of MECL while on the other hand  merely Rs. 10.00 crore is provided for VRS instead of the actual requirement of Rs. 30.00
crore. The Committee feels that the insistence of the Ministry of Mines to keep the financial restructuring pending for some time till 500 more
employees are separated from the Company does not reflect the positive attitude of the Ministry of Mines regarding the possible revival and
resurrection of MECL.  The Committee is of the strong view that  the Ministry of Mines should not adopt dilly-dallying  approach and attitude in
forwarding and pursuing  the Comprehensive Financial Restructuring proposal to the Ministry of Finance.  And it is expected that the Ministry of
Finance should give due consideration for sanctioning the restructuring proposal.

16.0                 Fiscal Issues Pertaining to Mining Industry
16.1     Reacting to the budget proposals 2003-04 the representatives of FIMI highlighted the following issues:-
“The marginal rationalization of freight in Railway Budget 2003-04 has provided some relief to the industry.  However, there has not been any
significant rationalization in the tax and duty structure to benefit the mining industry.
16.2     Some of the changes are as follows:-
(i)
                  Custom duty on nickel has been unified at 10% from 5% and 15% irrespective of the class of importer.
(ii)                Custom duty on lead has been reduced from 25% to 20%.
(iii)               Special Additional Duty of Customs (SAD) has been exempted on rock phosphate and sulphur.
(iv)              Excise duty on articles made of mica has been rationalized which will give marginal boost to the crisis ridden mica sector.
(v)                Special Additional duty of Customs (SAD) has been exempted on rock phosphate and sulphur rock phosphate is of low grade and cost of
production and/or beneficiation being higher it will affect the domestic industry by encouraging imports into the country.
(vi)              The major impact on the mining industry would be the rise in fuel cost i.e. diesel as minerals are low value, high volume commodity
where any slight change in the freight would have significant impact.”
16.3              The mining or the mineral industry has not received any boost with the current budget provisions.  The lower custom duty had poised
severe threat on the sustainability of certain minerals like graphite and therefore it was suggested that the customs duty should be revised upwards
to safeguard the Indian industry from cheap imports as the cost of production in India is high because of high power and infrastructure cost. 
However, no relief has been extended to such minerals.
 
16.4                 The representatives of Federation of Indian Mineral Industries in the Committee’s meeting held on 27 th March 2003 and the Ministry
of Mines apprised the Committee through its Pre-budget Papers and expectations of Mining Industry from the budget (2003-04) that the Multi
Disciplinary Committee, constituted by the Ministry of Mines in April 1998 to study the taxation regime in the mining sector,  has given a number of
recommendations for bringing about fiscal priorities between Petroleum and Coal Sectors however, despite the best efforts of the Ministry of Mines
to consider the recommendations for including in the Budget have not received the favorable response of the Ministry of Finance. The major issues
include:-
(i)
      Rate of annual depreciation for mining plant and equipment should be increased to 100 percent.
(ii)    All expenditure incurred prior to commercial production including the expenditure incurred on site and deposit acquisition should be eligible for
amortization over the minimum mining lease period of 20 years or a lesser period at the  option of the lessee.
(iii)   For reclamation of mined out area, the mining companies may be allowed to earmark a percentage of book profits each year to meet
rehabilitation cost in future and set it aside as a special reserve in their books.
(iv)  Import duties on mining equipment may be reduced for equipment used for gold and diamond mining operations nil duty should be applicable
while for to other mining operations the duty should be at par with imports for coal mining.
(v)    Nil levy of excise duty structure for concentrate produced in the leaseholds and low excise duty structure for concentrates produced outside
leaseholds, may be devised.
(vi)  Declaration of ores, minerals and concentrates as “declared goods” under Central Sales Tax Act to limit the Sales Tax rate to 4 percent.
(vii)Abolishing or compounding of local levies, which are not conducive for free flow of goods.
(viii)
           State governments may not insist on equity sharing with investing companies.
16.5                 The Ministry of Mines submitted the recommendations of the Multi Disciplinary Committee to the Ministry of finance for its approval
in July 2000, however, the matter is still pending in the Ministry of Finance

16.6                 The Multi Disciplinary Committee on taxation regime for Mineral Sector in the country in its report submitted in July 2002, reiterated
its recommendations for suitable amendment in the Section 35E of the Income Tax Act for providing that all expenditure incurred prior to
commercial production including the expenditure incurred on site and development acquisition should be eligible for amortization over  the minimum
lease period at the option of lessee.
16.7                 Pertaining to the extension of benefits of Section 33ABA of the Income Tax Act, 1961, inserted w.e.f. 1 st April, 1999 (where a
provision of a site restoration fund has been provided for the petroleum and natural gas sector) for the mining sector in general, with the modification
that for reclamation of mined out areas, the mining companies may be allowed to earmark a percentage of book profits each year to meet the
rehabilitation cost in future and set aside as a special reserve in their books, the Multi Disciplinary Committee opined that:-
“Reclamation of mined out area to its original position involves huge investment which usually takes place at the end of mine life when there is no
come.   The extent of rehabilitation activities is clearly mentioned in the mining plan and environment management plan approved by the IBM and
oEF respectively and is also regulated by these authorities.  Expenditure on site restoration can be as high as 25% of the total project cost.  These are
gitimate expenses and need to be allowed as in the case of petroleum sector which provides the modalities for availing the deduction for exploration
d production for Companies that have concluded Production sharing contracts with the Government of India.  Introduction of similar provisions would
able non-fuel mining companies to provide for rehabilitation costs.  However, the requirement of maintaining a bank accounts as is the case of
troleum sector where the funds are deposited should be discarded as this creates an added cash constraint for the companies.  It is recommended that in
ace of this, the mining companies may be allowed to earmark a percentage of book profits each year to meet rehabilitation costs in future. 
eductibility may be permitted based on the amounts, set aside in a specific reserve created for the purpose in the books of account, instead of any
quirement to set the money abide in a separate bank account.”
16.8                 As regards the exemption of excise duty in the beneficiation of Ores it was stated that Ore and minerals are exempt from excise duty. 
Beneficiation of the ores yields ‘concentrates’ by reduction or removal of impurities to make it suitable as input raw material for subsequent
metallurgical or chemical or extractive operations.  Thus beneficiation of ore is a preparatory process for manufacture, not involving actual
manufacture.  Therefore, it is recommended that concentrates produced through beneficiation of ores within leasehold areas may be exempt from
levy of excise duty in the same manner as ores and minerals.
16.9                 The representative of  FIMI elaborated on the rational custom structure for mining industry and suggested following pattern of custom
duty:-
(i)
                  There should be an increase in duty on unwrought metal and aluminium semi-fabricated products including scrap.
(ii)                Since Zinc is strategic metal the duty on Zinc concentrates as well as scrap should be increased to provide assistance to the domestic industry
which has been suffering for high power and freight cost.
(iii)               Since Copper is used extensively in a wide variety of critical sectors i.e. telecommunications, power, railways, defence, space research etc.
and 75% of India’s demand for this vital strategic material was being met through imports, therefore, (a)Customs duty on refined copper (copper
cathodes, wire bars and CC rods) should be increased from present level and customs duty on copper concentrates should be nil(b) There should
be single uniform customs duty rate levied on imports of copper cathodes, wire bars and CC rods (c) Customs duty on copper scrap imports
should be at same rate as customs duty on copper cathodes, wire bar and CC rods.
 
16.10               The Committee after having  giving  a proper thought to the fiscal related proposals as suggested by FIMI and the Ministry of Mines
has arrived at the conclusion  that the Ministry of Finance should give due consideration to the following items for the rapid growth and development
of mining sector:-
(i)
                  In regard to the Section 35E of the Income Tax Act, 1962, the costs incurred during the pre production period should be amortizable from
the year of commencement of commercial production over the balance period of mining lease, or a lesser period at the option of the lessee. 
Accordingly, therefore, all expenditure incurred prior to commercial production including the expenditure incurred on site and development
acquisition should be eligible for amortization over the minmum lease period of 20 years or a leser period at the option of the lessee.  The section
35E of the Income Tax Act, 1961 can be suitably amended accordingly without significant and immediate financial implications.
(ii)
                The Committee is in agreement with the view of the Ministry of Mines for extension of benefits of Section 33ABA of the Income Tax Act,
1961, inserted w.e.f. 1st April, 1999 (where a provision of a site restoration fund has been provided  for the petroleum and natural gas sector) for
the mining sector in general, with the modification that for reclamation of mined out areas, the mining companies may be allowed to earmark a
percentage of book profits each year to meet the rehabilitation cost in future and set aside as a special reserve in their books.
(iii)
               Concentrates produced through beneficiation of ores within leasehold areas may be exempt from levy of excise duty in the same manner as
ores and minerals.
(iv)              There should be no change in the duty structure on copper concentrate, copper cathodes, copper wire bars and CC rods and copper scraps.
(v)                The rates of custom duty on aluminum scrap, primary and secondary aluminum may be maintained at the existing rate.
(vi)              The Zinc  industry to be also allowed the concessional lower custom duty on metallurgical coke.
(vii)             There should be a minimum duty differential of 10% between lead and lead acid batteries, which is at present only 5%.
16.11      The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Finance should give favorable consideration to the fiscal related suggestions of the
Committee and the Ministry of Mines should leave no stone unturned in convincing the Ministry of Finance.
 
17.0                 Requirement of restructuring in infrastructure  of Mining sector
17.1     The representative of FIMI apprised the Committee that although at present the per unit cost of production in Indian mines remain quite

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA

competitive vis-à-vis in other major mining countries in the world, the Indian industry has suffered heavily because of the lack of and the cost of
infrastucture.  There are hardly any worth-while roads in the mining areas.  Whatever roads are available are for the general public which are also
used for the movement of the mineral ores.
17.2     The Committee is in complete agreement with the views of FIMI  that there are no dedicated railway line either to a mineral company or for
any mineral.  For the movement of minerals over long distance.  One takes the help of the railway facilities which are government-owned and
woefully inadequate.  The size of the rake as well as rate of freight are no way near the world standards.
17.3                 The Committee approves the suggestions given by FIMI that following measures should taken up at the earliest for facilitating the
bulk movements of minerals:-
(i)
      Expeditious completion of Daitan-keonjhar-banspani (DKB) railway project within the stipulated time frame so as to reduce the rail distance
from iron ore producing areas of Jharkhand and Orissa to Paradip Port.
(ii)    For dispatch of iron ore from bailadila Sector to various producers of pig iron/sponge iron/steel plants in Chhattisgarh, Madhya Prdesh,
Maharashtra and Gujarat, Jagdalpur-Rowghat-Durg rail line should be established.
(iii)   Tori-Shivpur-Barkagaon-Bhurkunda, Pirpathi-Seori and gua-Manoharpur via Chiria rail projects need to be completed on priority.
(iv)  Construction of railway line between Hubli and Ankola, a distance of 172 kms. Which will reduce the lead from Bellary-Hospet by 200 kms.
And make iron ore from this area competitive in the world market.
17.4                 The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Mines should seriously pursue the rail related infrastructure development for mining
sector with the Railways:-
17.5                 As regards the standardization of port facilities and moderanization of equipment and technology of various ports, the FIMI was of the
view that port charges go on increasing but their capacity to handle decreases with the passage of time.  There is no replacement of handling
equipments.  Moreover except Vizag and Chennai ports, capacity of other ports are only to accept vessels upto a maximum of 60,000 DWT.  Because
of the initiative and enterprising spirit of the private Goan exporters.  Murmugao Port is able to handle larger vessels by mid-stream loading through
barges and transhipers.  In the ports like Vizag and Chennai, there are constant break-downs of handling equipments basically because these
equipments have not have replaced over the last many years.
17.6                 The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Mines should take up the matter with the Ministry of Shipping for standardlisation
of port facilities and moderanization of equipment and technology of various ports for rendering appropriate service to the Mining Sector.
17.7                 The representatives of FIMI highlited the lack of co-ordinated approach for development of infrastructural facilities for mining sector
highlighting the fact that there are different departments for each of these infrastructure facilities who work in different directions with hardly any
coordination.  The inadequacy and high cost of infrastructure continue to be the single greatest hurdle to the growth of mineral exports and the
development of the mineral sector as a whole.  With opening of the economy and more demand for minerals, it is imperative that some rationalization
will have to be made in these areas.  There has to be restructuring in infrastructure sector as well.  The speed with which these can be affected will
depend on the scale of development and demand for minerals in the country either for domestic consumption and/or for exports.
17.8                 The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Mines has to prove its mettle in performing its role as a facilitator and co-ordinator
in-tandem with various Departments of Government for providing the mining sector the appropriate infrastructure at cost effective rate for speedy
movement of the minerals. The call of the restructuring  in infrastructure sector is a genuine demand on the part of the representatives of mineral
associations.  The Government has already given due impetus and consideration to the development of infrastructure sector in the budget 2003-04. 
However, it depends upon the proficiency of the Ministry of Mines as to how much resources it can pull for development of infrastructure in regard
to mining sector.  Therefore, it’s the time for  Ministry of Mines to buck up.

20.1        The SWOT analysis of the Mining Sector in India reveal the following:
Strength Weaknesses
Mining plays a crucial role in the industrial development of 
the country. 
 
India has a vast geological potential, and has been gifted by 
nature with a variety of minerals, comprising 4 fuel 
minerals, 11 metallic minerals, 52 non metallic minerals and 
22 minor minerals.
 
Mining sector provides employment to more than one 
million people 
 
 Mineral exports constitute 16% of India's total exports.
 
India has a large pool of mining engineers, managers and 
skilled workers.
 
 
India has a strong and established legal system and 
commercial law practices, which is conducive to building 
investor confidence.
 
 
Mineral exploration is a high cost and high-risk activity. 
 
Mining faces competing demand on surface rights for mineral bearing area- viz 
forest, agriculture, buildings
 
Mining industry  faces high incidence of taxes.
 
Local concerns often override national concerns in granting of mineral concessions 
in States. 
 
Mining has a general public image of being an environmentally degrading  industry
 
Quality mineral deposits many a times are located in Forest areas/tribal areas
 
 
Opportunities Threats
India has favourable geological configuration, being part of 
the original Gondwana land mass comprising Australia, 
Africa and Antarctic, all identified mineral rich areas.
 
India has a history of mineral occurrences, including base 
metals, precious stones and diamonds.
India is one of the many investment destinations for global investment.  In order to 
maintain the geological advantage, India needs to compete seriously to attract 
higher share of already shrinking global exploration expenses.
 
Aggressive and malicious activism against mining by environment activists.

granting conditional mining leases for setting up mineral base industries in the 
State, even if the mining concern does not have core competence in such industries, 
or the State does not have adequate infrastructure to sustain such industries.

21.0     Impact of globalisation and liberalization
 
21.1     Since 1994, in a twin strategy, the Government has liberalized the legal framework for the mining regime, as well as progressively opened up
the mining and mineral sector for foreign investment. Statutory amendments have been carried out by which greater powers have been delegated to
the States for streamlining the mining regime, along with  security of tenure for the investors, for globalising the  Indian mineral sector, the policy
regime concerning foreign direct investment has been made more liberal. Since February 2000, all proposals for foreign direct investment in the
mining sector are eligible for automatic approval, subject to ceilings on foreign equity on the mineral concerned for such approval. Except for
precious stones and diamonds, automatic approval of foreign direct investment up to 100% is permissible for gold, silver and all other non-fuel and
non-atomic minerals. For precious stones and diamonds, automatic approval for foreign direct investment is permissible up to 74%.  In response to
the policy initiatives, Government approvals have been granted in respect of 72 applications, involving a proposed foreign direct investment (FDI)
induction worth Rs.4018 crore. Under the mining statutes, the foreign companies bringing in the FDI have to incorporate Indian subsidiary
Companies for being eligible to take mineral concessions, and therefore impact of globalisation and liberalization in the mining sector can be
indicated by the seriousness evinced by the Companies, who were permitted to bring in foreign investment by the Government in taking mineral
concessions. 
 
21.2     In 1997, the Ministry of Mines had issued guidelines to facilitate large area aerial prospecting, in response to which, the entrepreneurs have
taken 65 large area prospecting licenses, covering an area of over 90 thousand square kilometers. After the amendment in the MMDR Act, 1957 in
1999, 119 Reconnaissance Permits covering an area of over 155 thousand square kilometers have been granted as on date.
 
21.3     The Committee is pleased to note that the Government has liberalized the legal framework for the mining regime, as well as progressively
opened up the mining and mineral sector for foreign investment. Statutory amendments have been carried out by which greater powers have been
delegated to the States for streamlining the mining regime, along with  security of tenure for the investors, for globalising the  Indian mineral sector,
the policy regime concerning foreign direct investment has been made more liberal.  The Committee notes that  all proposals for foreign direct
investmentup to 100% in the mining sector, except for precious stones and diamonds, are eligible for automatic approval.   However, the Committee
is of the view that the Ministry of Mines should undertake comparative study of the legal frame work of countries leading in Mining activities and
mull out the relevant provisions for incorporating the same in the Indian Mining legal frame work.  The Committee further recommends that the
Ministry of Mines should also study the negative impact of globalization and liberalization and must  undertake suitable and resilient measure for
over coming the negative impact of globalization and liberalization on the Mining Sector.
 
21.4     The representatives of FIMI pointed out that there is practically no change in the attitude of the State Governments.  No rationalization of
procedures of transparency is evident.  There are inordinate delays in processing of applications and there are no serious efforts to reduce it.  Political
interference and red- tapism in decision making has added another dimension.  There is virtually no infrastructure no good roads, hardly any power

22.0     “ Key concern Areas of Mining Industry”
 
22.1     National Mineral Policy,1993(NMP) was formulated to  recognise  the need for encouraging  private investment including foreign direct
investment and  State -of –the – Art technology in the mineral sector. A number of  amendments  have been made in the statute  governing the Indian
mineral sector and the rules framed there under in order to make  the sector hassle free and investor friendly.
 
22.2     It has been felt that although  the legal frame work in the mining sector  is now  comparable  to the best  in  the world the fiscal regime
governing the mining sector , particularly relating  to expenses over exploration etc needs a lot of improvement. Beside involvement/clearance of  a
number of  agencies in grant of mineral concession before  final commencement of  actual operation is also  flagged as a deterrent. .
 
22.3  To make the taxation regime for  the mineral sector  at par with best in the world, a Multi Disciplinary Committee (MDC) was constituted by
Ministry of  Mines  in 1998. Recommendations of the MDC  were accepted  by the Ministry and sent to Ministry of Finance  for adoption. Nothing
positive has so far been heard from Ministry of Finance. Acceptance of the recommendations of the MDC would certainly make mining globally
competitive.
 
22.4     The Committee while expresses its satisfaction to know that the legal frame-work in mining sector is comparable to the best in the world,
however,  high cost of exploration is a matter of concern.  The Committee is of the view that adequate research and development activities and
employment of modern tools and techniques would certainly bring down the cost of exploration.
 
22.5     So far as the involvement of a number of agencies  in the grant of mineral concessions before the commencement of  actual operation acting
as a deterrent factor is concerned, it is suggested that the Ministry of Mines should  come forward with the proposal /suggestions for the absolutely 
required structures, stages and process for the grant of Mineral concession vis-à-vis the existing system.   The Committee is of the view that there
should be minimum time gap during the process of  grant of mineral concession, clearance from the Ministry  of Environment and Forest  and the
final commencement of actual operation.
 
22.6     The Committee is constrained to express its deep concern over the fact that the recommendations  of  the Multi Disciplinary Committee
MCD, constituted by the Ministry of Mines in 1998 to look into a taxation regime suitable to the mineral sector, is long pending in the Ministry of
Finance.  The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Mines should pursue the matter with the Department of Revenue( Ministry of Finance and
Company Affairs).  Since the Ministry of Mines has already examined  and accepted the recommendations of Multi Disciplinary Committee and it
has been found that the recommendations of the Multi Disciplinary Committee contains the potential and strategy for making Mining Sector globally
competitive, it is expected that  one wing of the Government has the co-ordination and consensus-aid-idem with the another wing, the Department of
Revenue would give due consideration to the recommendation of Multi Disciplinary Committee without  further loss of time. 
 
23.0     LATEST TREND IN MINING SECTOR IN INDIA
23.1     During  April, December, 2002, the Index of Mineral Production for the minerals administered under the Mineral Conservation and
Development Rules, 1988 (MCDR,1988) stood at 149.78 which marked an increase of 13.90%  over the index for the corresponding period in 2001. 
It can be said therefore that the overall production of the mineral which are overseen by the Ministry of Mines has been satisfactory in 2002-03.  The
economics of metallic minerals, prices of which are linked to international prices faced difficulty in 2002-03  since the prices prevailing in the 
London Metal Exchange (LME) were quite low in 2002-03.  The LME  price for zinc is prevailing at only $ 750-770 per tonne, as against about $ 
1200  two years ago.  The LME price for lead is around $ 450 per tonne, while it was around $ 490 two years ago.  For aluminium, the LME price is
around $ 1380 per tonne as against $ 1550  only two years ago.   Similarly copper concentrate price is around $1554 per tonne while it was $ 1806 
per tonne two years ago.

Fiscal Issues Pertaining to Mining Industry
 
                        The Committee after having giving a proper thought to the fiscal related proposals as suggested by FIMI and the Ministry of Mines
has arrived at the conclusion  that the Ministry of Finance should give due consideration to the following items for the rapid growth and development
of mining sector:-
(i)
                  In regard to the Section 35E of the Income Tax Act, 1962, the costs incurred during the pre production period should be amortizable
from the year of commencement of commercial production over the balance period of mining lease, or a lesser period at the option of the
lessee.  Accordingly, therefore, all expenditure incurred prior to commercial production including the expenditure incurred on site and
development acquisition should be eligible for amortization over the minmum lease period of 20 years or a leser period at the option of the
lessee.  The section 35E of the Income Tax Act, 1961 can be suitably amended accordingly without significant and immediate financial
implications.
(ii)
                The Committee is in agreement with the view of the Ministry of Mines for extension of benefits of Section 33ABA of the Income Tax
Act, 1961, inserted, 1st April, 1999 (where a provision of a site restoration fund has been provided  for the petroleum and natural gas sector)
for the mining sector in general, with the modification that for reclamation of minded out areas, the mining companies may be allowed to
earmark a percentage of book profits each year to meet the rehabilitation cost in future and set aside as a special reserve in their books.
(iii)               Concentrates produced through beneficiation of ores within leasehold areas may be exempt from levy of excise duty in the same manner
as ores and minerals.
(iv)              There should be no change in the duty structure on copper concentrate, copper cathodes, copper wire bars and CC rods and copper
scraps.
(v)                The rates of custom duty on aluminum scrap, primary and secondary aluminum may be maintained at the existing rate.

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, 
having   been authorized by the Committee, hereby present this One Hundred Twenty –Fourth      Report 
on the Demands for Grants (2003-04) pertaining to the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries  
2.         The Committee heard the oral evidence of the Secretary and other representatives of the Ministry
of Agro and Rural Industries on 31 st March, 03. The Committee also considered the pre- budget 
expectation and post budget reactions of   the Ministry of Agro and Ru ral Industries to have in-depth 
account of the impact of budget  proposals (2003-04) on the Agro an d Rural Industries a as whole , 
including  units in private sector.  
3. The Committee examined the relevant documents and  budget -papers furnished by the Ministry . The 
Committee is thankful to the repres entatives of Ministry of Agro and Rural Indus tries    who appeared
before the Committee.  The Committee also wishes to  thank the Ministry  for furnishing the replies to
the questionnaire and the points raised during the course of   oral evidence.   
4.         The Committee at its meeting held on   6th May 03 considered and adopted the Report. 
 
  
  
REPORT 
Agro and Rural Industries play an important role in national economy because of the vast
potential of this sector in terms of sustainable employment generation and dispersal of industries in rural
areas. With the onset of globalizat ion and liberalized econom ic scenario in the country, the Agro and
Rural Industries Sector has been envisaged and acknowledged as one  of the major avenues available for
creation of employment and to en sure balanced economic growth.  Added to the already existing
regional imbalances, opening up of the economy to ma rket   forces with mi nimum control mechanisms,
was a real and potent threat to at taining the avowed objective of balanced economic development. Since
this sector is the major non-farm sector with a vast potential to create and sustain employment across the 
country, specifically the backward and rural areas it is necessary to reinforce and strengthen the
functioning of the sector as a whole, by highlighting its presen t status and ensu ring timely policy
interventions needed. Further streamlining by way of  restructuring field agen cies and the sector’s 
competitive policy positioning has enhanced its inhe rent strength to forge ah ead and ensure balanced
growth.  
1.1       In view of the growing significance of Agro and Rural Industries, the Ministry of Agro & Rural
Industries was carved out of the erstwhile Ministry of  Small Scale Industri es and Agro & Rural
Industries   w.e.f. 1 st September 2001. The need was felt for carving out a Se parate Ministry because 
ofthe increasing criticality of the sector in the libe ralized economic set up needed  to be reinforced. As a
major sector with vast employmen t potential on a sustainable basis exploiting optimally the indigenous
wealth available especiall y by way of traditional craft and t echniques, a separate Ministr y of A gro &

Rural Industries was a necessity, which was formally recognized.  
  
1.2       The Committee understands that Agro and Rural Industries has tremendous scope and potential 
for gainful employment and boosting ba lanced economic growth and development thereby changing the
status of India’s developing econom y to a developed economy keeping in  view the fact that the large
chunk of India’s population resi de in rural areas.   The onus lies on the Ministry of ARI, carved out o f 
the erstwhile Ministry  of SSI and ARI on 1 st September 2001, to translate th is dream into a reality by
undertaking key issues concerning the Agro and Rural Industries synergistically and effectively. 
1.3       The main function of the Ministry is to  formulate policy measures for the growth of rural
industries for achieving rapid increase in gainful employment and balanced re gional growth, which are
among the main objectives underlying th e strategy of industrialization in the country. It also supervises
and coordinates the activities of different promotional agencies operating at the Central and State Level. 
The Ministry acts as a nodal agency for promotion and development of village and cottage industries as
well as tiny and micro enterprises in  both urban and rural areas.  The Charter for the Ministry describes
its objective as one to promote, ai d and foster growth of Agro a nd Rural Industries by providing them
institutional support in the areas  of marketing, export, technol ogy upgradation, training and common
facility services.  The constituents in the Ministry are:- 
(i)                  K&VI sector, 
(ii)                Coir sector,  
(iii)               Tiny and Micro Enterprises. 
1.4       Field agencies that implement policies and programmes relating to this sector are:- 
(i)                  Khadi & Village Industries Commission (KVIC) 
(ii)                Coir Board, 
(iii)               Office of DC (SSI) and 
(iv)              PMRY division.  
1.5       The Committee notes the structural   ar rangement of Ministry of ARI and at the same time
expects that all the field agencies, i.e. KVIC, Coir Board, office  of DC (SSI) and PMRY division would
perform their respective assigned task effectively a nd efficiently.   In this context, the Committee
recommends that all the wings of Ministry of ARI would discharge their functions and responsibilities in
such a manner that Agro and Rural Sector in ge neral may contribute to national economic growth and
development.  
1.6       The Ministry guides and coordinates with the implementing agencies to ensure development and
achievement as per the set mandate.T he Ministry has three-pronged role to play ,all of which aim at 
quality implementation of policies, programmes and sc hemes of the Ministry. In  the role of a policy
maker, the Ministry collects, collates and derives infe rences, which act as critic al input to further policy
formulation/amendments. In the role  of an advocate, the Ministry a dvocates and puts up ‘felt needs’ o f 
the stakeholders involved in the sector  as a whole. In the role of a fa cilitator, the Ministry facilitates,
coordinates and supports its fi eld agencies in implementing the programmes and schemes both
quantitatively and qualitatively. 
1.7       At present, the monitoring mechanism at the Ministry level includes both structured as well as
informal but regular monitori ng. Committee headed by Secretar y (ARI) periodically monitors
implementation of PMRY. A sim ilar Committee is being consti tuted for monitoring programmes
implemented by KVIC. At present, KVIC’s work is monitored based on their monthly progress report as
well as frequent interactions held  between the KVIC and Ministry at various levels.Work of Coir Board
is monitored on similar li nes as well as throu gh its board meetin gs. Measures, which would make the

Ministry’s role more effective and efficient, would be  frequent informal interactions with field agencies
and structured inputs from local public representatives. 
1.8              The Committee notes that the Ministry of ARI is entruste d with the functions/duties o f 
implementations of policies, prog rammes and schemes and in turn play the role of a policy maker,
advocate and a facilitator.  The Committee also finds that the Ministry monitors the activities undertaken
by its field’s agencies through formal  structure as well as informal meetings.  However, the Committee
is of the view that the Ministry  of ARI would act promptly as a policy maker, advocate and facilitato r
and promote Agro and Rural I ndustries by effective implementat ion of policies programmes and
schemes undertaken by its various field agencies without time a nd cost over run.  The existing
monitoring mechanism must ensure th at targets are achieved within th e stipulated time frame.  The
Committee further recommends that  the Ministry of ARI should have  review meetings  of its field
agencies to take stock of the progress made in the implementation of various schemes and programmes.

7.0       Prime Minister’s Rozgar Yojana. 
7.1       The Prime Minister’s Rozgar Yojana was announced by the Prime Minister on 15th August 1993 
for creation of sustainable self -employment opportunities for th e educated unemployed youth. The 
objective of the Prime Minister’s Ro zgar Yojana (PMRY) is to miti gate the problem of unemployment 
amongst the educated  unemployed youth through se tting up of self-employe d tiny units. The scheme 
came into operation on 2 nd October, 1993. The scheme was designe d to provide employment to more 
than a million persons by setting up of 7 lakh mi cro-enterprises by the educated unemployed youth 
during the 8th five year Plan. These self-employment ventures  were to be set up through industry,
services & business routes. It was envisaged that on an av erage each enterprise .set up would generate
employment for 2 persons.  As reported by the RB I, 7.748 lakh persons have been sanctioned loans
under PMRY, since its inception during the 8th five year Plan. The scheme continued in the 9"' five yea r 
Plan and the scheme is continuing during 10th Five Year Plan.

8.0       STRENGTHS, WEAKNESSES,  OPPORTUNITIES AN D THREADS (SWOT)
ANALYSIS OF PMRY. 
Strengths: 
                  1.            The spread of the Scheme is uni form in both urban as well as  rural areas of the country. As
per the findings of the second round of the evaluation on the PMRY disbursement of the
beneficiaries in rural and urban areas is 49.9% and 50.1% respectively. 
                  2.            Against the target of 18 lakh, loans have been  sanctioned to 20.40 lakh and disbursed to 
16.00 lakh educated unempl oyed youth between 1993-94 – 2001-02.  Employment 
opportunities have been  estimated to be created for about 24 lakh people during the same
period. 
                  3.            According to 2nd round of Evaluation study, assets that have been created is 89.7% of cases 
disbursed loan. 
Weaknesses: 
Declining recovery rate: 
                  1.            The recovery of loan overdue s under the PMRY Scheme has been declining.  It was 37.2
per cent for the half year ending March 2000 and has come down to 34.8 per cent for the half
year ending March 2002.   
                  2.            The overall amount of loan di sbursed under the Scheme has been stagnating around Rs.57,
000/- to Rs.58, 000/- per beneficiar y despite enhancement in th e maximum project cost from
Rs.1 lakh to Rs.2 lakh. 
                  3.            There is gap between number of cases sanctioned and disbursed by banks.

                  1.            In a situation where employme nt opportunities in organized sectors and Govt. sectors have

for achieving the basic objectives of the programme in a time bound frame.

 9.15    Evaluation and objective Assessment of PMRY 
Replying to the committee’s query  as to  the states where PMRY was a full all success; the 
states where PMRY did marginally good and the st ates where PMRY failed miserably, along with
reasons for such performance, the Ministry of Agro and Rural I ndustries stated the States where PMRY
was a full all success are Punjab and Himachal Pradesh (disburseme nt vis-à-vis targets is 80% an d 
above).  The States where PMRY is working satisfactorily are Haryana, Rajasthan, M.P. U.P.,
Maharashtra, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Pondicherry, Lakshadweep etc. (i.e. disbursement vis-à-
vis targets is 60% & above).  The States where PMRY has failed ar e: Delhi, J&K, West Bengal and
North Eastern States e.g. Manipur , Meghalaya, Nagaland, Tripura and Arunachal Pradesh etc. (i.e.
disbursement vis-à-vis targets ar e 30 pr cent or less). The States where disbursement under the Scheme
is 80% and above those States wh ere recovery of loan overdues is  around 55%. (Punjab – 57.3 per cent 
for the half year ended March 2001) . The States where the Scheme has been implemented satisfactorily
are the States where th e recovery of loan overdues is between 40 per cent to 45 per cent.  (i.e. Haryana
43.1 per cent; U.P. 45.6 percent; Rajasthan 42.1 per cent; Gujarat 61.2 per cent; Karnataka 48.1 per cent
for the half year ended March 2001).  The States where disbursements are less than 30% of the target are
the States where recovery of loan overdues is very low.  The recovery of lo an overdues for the period
ending March, 2001 was 1.0 per cent in Manipur 1.7 per cent in Nagaland; 13.0 per cent in Assam; 16.7
per cent in West Ben gal for the half year ended March, 2001.  In  J&K, the recovery of loan overdues is

Weakness:

The marketing strategy of KVIC is to focus on its eco friendly and natural product range. Khadi

basically cover local area needs and marketing is not much of a problem. With rega rd to non-consumer 
goods normally units established have good market as most of such products are intermediary products
used by other industries. Main di fficulty is in consumer goods a nd khadi. For both these products areas
of intervention involves a detail ed marketing strategy for publicit y, branding and brand promotion,
design input, better packaging etc.  Accessing private marketing cha nnel, modernization of existing
channels, organizing large scale e xhibitions are important aspects. Marketing federations have been
formed with various village industries federations to  act as facilitator outsi de the governmental set up.

12.28   COST REDUCTION OF COIR PRODUCTS 
            Under the cluster development activ ities, Coir Board proposes to promote the formation o f
consortium among the smal l scale manufacturers and small and medium exporte rs so as to have a

reduce the selling cost of the pr oducts to the minimum extent po ssible.  Under the UNDP Project

effective manner.  It is proposed to replicate the strategy in other coir producing sectors by the Board.

12.33   COOPERATIVISATION SCHEME 
12.33.1            The objectives of the co-operati visation scheme were forma tion of viable coir co-
operatives and revitalisation of the potentially viable dormant societies and bringing the coir workers in
to the co-operative fold so that the quality a nd quantity of production impr oves, workers get bette r
wages and they are freed from e xploitation of middlemen and the i ndustry is put on a sound footing.  It
was aimed to bring 80% of the work-force in the industry under co-operative  fold through of the 
scheme. Coir Board is the m onitoring agency of the Scheme.             The objectives of the scheme are
yet to be achieved due to a mult iplicity of reasons. The Institut e of Rural Management which had
conducted an evaluative study on th e scheme, opined that the “Schem e of Co-operativisation in Coi r 
Industry as it is envisaged and implemented need s to undergo drastic revision to meet the emerging
challenges. The Integrated Coir Development Project is one of the components of the Co-operativisation 
Scheme.  It envisages setting up of new primary co-operatives, modernisation and expansion of existing 
co-operatives, improved handlooms, curling units and automatic spinni ng units etc.   The Project is 
being implemented with the assistance of National Co-operative Development Corporation (NCDC) and 
the coir producing States concerned. Assistance under this component is still being released.   
12.33.2            The Committee is of view that  the objectives of the co- operativisation scheme i.e. 
formation of viable coir co-operatives and revitalizat ion of the potentially viab le dormant societies and 
bringing the coir workers in to the co-operati ve fold  for improving th e quality and quantity o f 
production and putting industry on a sound footing is a unique mission in Coir Industry.    Therefore, the
suggestion of the Institute of Rural Management  that the Scheme of Co-operativisation in Coir Industry 
as it is envisaged and implemen ted needs to undergo drastic revisi on to meet the emerging challenges,
needs attention of the government . The National Co-operative Deve lopment Corporation (NCDC) may 
be entrusted with greater role for implementation of co-operativisation scheme. 
12.34   Model Coir Village Scheme  
12.34.1            Coir Board has been implement ing the Model Coir Village Scheme from the year 1983
which provides assistance to coir workers to improve their working and living conditions.  The
assistance is provided to coir wo rkers in all coir producing States/U Ts of the country.  During the last
three years, no villages were a dopted under the Scheme as the Mini stry did not accord sanction fo r
continuation of the scheme afte r 1999-2000.  In 1999, the Mi nistry entrusted the Institute of Rural
Management, Anand, Gujarat to conduct an evalua tive study on the implemen tation of the scheme. 
After conducting the study, the IRMA recommended that  the programme merits continuance because it
is the only one of its kind.  But it needs to be rest ructured.  In line with the recommendations of the
IRMA, the Board drafted and submitted a scheme na med Production Oriented Welfare Scheme for Coi r
Workers to the Ministry for approval. 
12.34.2            The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of ARI should approve the Production
Oriented Welfare Schemes for Coir Workers as the follow up programme of Model Coir Village Yojana
which was a unique Yojana.  After all the fruits of development must reach to the lowest rung of society
and of course the workers as well who are the actual warriors of industrialization process.  So long, India
remains a Welfare State,  the provisions for Welfa re measures must continue for carrying out the
constitutional obligations.   The Co mmittee agrees with the views of  Institute of Rural Management,
Anand, Gujarat for continuance of Model Coir Village Yojana.

 12.36.1           West Bengal and Orissa are ma jor coconut producing States in India and the Board is

12.37   Merger of Coconut Developm ent Board and Coir Board for bette r co-ordination and Integrated 
planning. 
12.37.1            Responding to the proposal of the merger of Coconut Development Board and Coi r
Board for better co-ordination a nd integrated planning, the Minist ry of ARI has communicated the
committee that the Coconut Development Board is concentrated on production of coconut while the
Coir Board is concentrated on coir fibre and allied products.  The raw- material for coir  industry is the 
coconut husk, a byproduct of coconut industry.  The focu s of the above Boards ar e different.  The coi r
industry by and large provides employment to 5,86,000 peopl e and it is an export oriented industry and
earn foreign exchange to the tune  of Rs.320 crores annually. The base of raw-material availability is 
expanded.  Technical know-how for coir industry is  lacking in the non-traditional coconut growing 
areas.  It is necessary to pr ovide the requisite technical guida nce through a professional body like Coi r
Board.   
12.37.2            The Coir Board as a separate commodity Board  could do only so much focusing
employment generation in rural areas, development of new pr oducts, skill development in non-
traditional areas, transfer of technology, etc. The me rger of Coir Board with Coconut Development
Board will lose its focus for ex clusive development of coir indus try and its positive results being
achieved. There are different types of natural fibres like bana na fibre, pineapple fibr e, sisal, bimal, etc.
available in various parts of the country.  No concerted effort has been made for the industrial use of  the
above natural fibres available in a bundance.  It is desirable to pursue   formation of a Hard Fibre Board
rather than clubbing the activitie s of Coir Board with the Coconut  Development Board.  This will
increase the employment opportunity in rural areas in all States including North-Eastern region.

15.1     The Finance Minister  in his budget speech of the year 1999-2000 announced a scheme called the 
National Programme on Rural Industr ialisation.  The purpose of the scheme is to set up 100 rural
industrial clusters in the country  every year so that it can boost up the rural economy by creating more
employment  avenues for the rural youth in the non -farm sector, and slow dow n the migration of the 
rural artisans to towns/cities. Th e 0ffice of the Developm ent Commissioner(Small Scale Industries) was
made the coordinating agency and the KVIC was envisage d to play an important role in setting up these
clusters as well as making good use of its extensive marketing outlets.  No fund was provided separately
for the programme and it was fe lt that various Ministries/ De partments are having their own
programmes in this area which could be coordi nated and their synergie s exploited for greate r
impact.Consequent upon the bifurcatio n of business between the Ministry  of SSI and Ministry of ARI,
the scheme is being coordinated by the Ministry  of ARI recently, sinc e Sep 2002. The programme is
being implemented by NABARD and SIDBI in 31 and 14 clusters respectively. So far KVIC has already
launched the programme in 22 clusters  The state wi se position of implementation  of the programme is
placed at annexure. 
15.2     In order to facilitate implementation of the programme, a scheme on NPRI ha s been formulated
which has a provision of extendi ng financial assistance of Rs. 5.0 lakhs per cluster. The budget
provision of Rs. 90 lakhs under the sche me  was reduced to      Rs. 63 lakhs at RE stage for 2002-03 as 
the proposals were not received from  the states/ UTs  and the quart erly expenditure was not made. 
During this year, i.e.  2002-03, 16 diagnostic study  proposals from 9 States/ UTs of Assam, Andaman &
Nicobar, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Kerala, Maharashtra, Orissa,  Tamil Nadu, and UP have been
approved at a cost of Rs. 8 lakhs  under the scheme on NPRI formulat ed by the Govt. of India. Funds
amounting to Rs. 8 lakhs  shall be  released after receiving requisi te information from them. The
proposals from other States/ UTs have  also been invited for financial assistance under the scheme. The
scheme on NPRI of the Ministry is basically formulated as a gap filling arra ngement. The majo r
implementing agencies of the programme are KVIC, SIDBI and NABARD.  
  
15.3     The NPRI is basically fo rmulated  to facilitate the fill ing up of crucial gaps and develop
infrastructural linkages  as an add on to schemes already being executed by  the implementing agencies,
i.e. KVIC, SIDBI , NABARD  and States. The former three agen cies are implementing this programme
from their own resources. However,  the financial support to states as  also to these agencies shall be
provided to the extent admissible. Th e Committee observes that National Pro gramme for Rural

15.4     The Committee desires that NPRI’s scope should not be limited to just as gap filling arrangement
and it’s thrust should be widened as  a full fledged programme.  The Committee feels that government’s 
intention is gradually moving in this direction, that’s why, the Planning Commission has also constituted
Task Force on rural industrialization.  Need is to have a holistic and co-ordinated approach.  
  
15.5     The Committee, however, desires to point out the lacuna  in NPRI by highlighting  the fact that
no fund has been specifically made for th e programme on the a ssumption that various
Ministries/Departments havi ng their own programmes would co-ordinate and synergies fo
r 
implementing the Programme.  The Committee notes that all the programme s/schemes, presently
scattered into various ministries. All these progr ammes are to be integrated and co-ordinated fo r 
injecting synergy into the program me for its sure success and timel y implementation. The Ministry o f
Argo and Rural Industries should be bracketed as the nodal Ministry as  the vanguard of NPRI.  The
most important aspects for successful  implementation of a programme is  the credit flow .  NPRI is a
programme without specific and separate fund.  This is the setb ack at the very inception stage. 
Therefore, the Committee recomme nds that a Common corpus Fund  should be made, and the money
which presently goes to various sc hemes under different De partments/Ministries, should be put in this
Corpus Fund  intended for Comprehensive and co-o rdinated efforts for ru ral industrialization and 
development.   
15.6     The Committee is extremely pained to note  that the provision of Rs. 90 lakhs under the Scheme
was reduced to Rs. 63 lakhs at RE stage for 2002- 03 as the proposals were  not received from the 
States/UTs and the quarterly e xpenditure was not made.  Adequa te Awareness Programme has to be
organized by the implementing agencies of the pr ogramme i.e. KVIC, SIDIBI and NABARD.  The
Service of Regional Rural Banks may also be presse d into in the implementation of NPRI.le in the
scheme.  
 15.7    SWOT analysis (strength Weakness, Opportunities and Threats) of NPRI 
15.7.1  The Committee was apprised of the SWOT analysis of NPRI which is mentioned under:- 
Strength: Providing Common Facilit ies in a Cluster, Financial Assistance for infrastructure,
Training Facilities & Providing Marketing Facilities, to create jobs under Non-farm sector. 
Weakness:  Non availability of good NGOs and implementing agen cies at the field level fo r
implementation at various stages/centers.. 
Opportunities:  Cluster Developm ent Programme, Thrust Areas for rural enterprises, Marketing
network & Brand Creation, Science & Technol ogy inputs for higher qua lity & productivity &
HRD input for rural entrepreneurship & skill upgradation. 
Threats: Threat from organized sector and globalisation of world market.  
15.7.2  The scheme is in the initial stage of implementation. The problems arising out of implementation
of the programme shall be taken care of from time to time.

should make use of the SWOT-ana lysis of NPRI and extract benef it of the programmes, overcome its

15.8     Rural entrepreneurs and skill up-gradation  
15.8.1  The rural entrepreneurs in  the clusters are being trai ned to the desired technological
advancements and skill upgradation for effective development of th e clusters. Scope of the scheme
covers extending financial assistan ce  for the purpose of diagnostic st udy of the cluster, demonstration
and development of modern tools and kits and vari ous other technical inputs, training and strengthening
of NGO/cluster agent, establishm ent of Common Facility Centres et c. Also the major implementing
agencies are providing training to the entrepreneurs and creating awar eness by way of  exhibitions/fai r
wherever required.  
  
15.8.2  The Committee is of the opinion that technol ogical advancement and skill up-gradation fo r 
effective development of the cluster is a must. 
             
15.9     Role of KVIC under NPRI 
15.9.1  The KVIC is envisaged to play an important role  in setting up these clus ters as well as making
good use of its extensive marketing out lets. KVIC had decided to take up 50 clusters every year. So fa r
KVIC has already launched the programme in 22 clusters. KVIC has introduced a common brand name,
viz. ‘ Sarvodaya’ for six products for intensifying ma rketing efforts in their schemes. Initially, the
Sarvodaya brand name is covering th e selected village industries products namely, toilet soap, agarbatti,
and honey, pickles spices. These products are being sold through sales outlets of KVIC. 
15.9.2  The Committee, while appreciating the role of KVIC in general in setting up of cluster an d
providing marketing network and br and endowment, desires that KVIC should intensify its Mission fo r
rural industrialization. 
15.10   Participation of private entrepreneurs in NPRI and popularization of NPRI 
15.10.1  NPRI is being implemented through States/UTs with the help of   State Level Implementation 
Committee and District Level Implementation Committee. These committees are having members of 
KVIC, SIDBI, and NABARD, lead bank representatives. At central level, the concerned ministries have 
been included in the constitution of Inter-ministerial Task Force. The programme is implemented 
through an implementing agency/nodal agency, which may be a local NGO with good past track record 
ensuring participation of private enterprise. The scheme is being publicised by involving participation of 
the State agencies and local NGOs. All the states have been notified for taking up the cluster 
development under the scheme. They are required to constitute and notify DLIC and SLIC and submit 
the proposals.  
  
15.10.2            The Committee hopes that part icipation of private entr epreneur and NGO’s would 
promote the cluster under NPRI.  Th e Committee further desires that  the State level implementation
Committee and district level Implementation Committee should play pro -active Role in implementation 
of NPRI.

15.11   Task Force to calibrate a coordinated approach to the issu e of rural Industrialization and

15.11.1            The Task Force Constitu ted on Promotion of Rural Technology by the Planning
Commission have similar objectives as that of the NPRI. Secretary (SSI&ARI) is the member of the
Task Force. The task force would enhance the focused and coherent perspective of rural industrialization
as a whole, based critically on technology inputs. It would also enable optimal synergistic coordination
amongst all agencies involved in this sector.     
  
15.11.2            The Committee expects that, the Secretary (SSI and ARI) being the member of Task

focused and co-horrent perspective of NPRI. 
  
15.12   The Committee concludes that the Government should make NPRI a National Mission and make 
it a time-bound programme and ensure its success through Integrated and co-ordinated planning.  Need 
of the hour is to charge in the priority of financial allocation i.e.  the  mobilization of resources in the 
right direction.  Rural Industrialization is a gateway of India’s modernization and development at grass-
root-level.  A substantial budgetary provision in NPRI would ensure India’s progress and development 
as the same would provide economic-Swaraj to millions of people.

inherent competitive and resilient nature of the Agro and Rural Industries sector as such.

honey production, traditional cr afts items, etc are so exclusive by nature that it offers immense export

20.7  CREDIT FLOW TO AGRO & RURAL INDUSTRIES 
20.7.1  Major credit flow to the Agro &Rural Industrie s is through financial inst itutions. Credit flow to
units in this sector is supported by way of Margin Money/subsidy/loan/working capital. The loan part is
accessed through the financial institutions and the subsidy and margin money part of the project is borne
form the budgetary allocations to  the concerned implementing ag ency. Problems by way of unviable
projects, cutting down financial size of the projects, lengthy procedural formalities are faced in general
by the beneficiaries or entrepreneurs in accessing credit for their units.  This may be, to a certain extent
linked to unsatisfactory r ecovery of finances advanced. Hence th e attempt is to constantly, vigorously
pursue recovery dues and at the same time ensure easy accessibility to new entrepreneurs.  
20.7.2  The Committee is of the view that continued institutional credit  flow to ARI Sector is a prio r
condition for the growth and development of Agro a nd Rural Industries, theref ore, it is suggested that
the government should take suitable steps for ch anging the mindsets of fi nancial institutions fo r
providing sufficient credit flow to all concerned im plementing agencies of Agro and Rural Industries so
that the benefits of the schemes and programme must reach to the lowest rungs of the society as is
intended at the initial stage of pol icy making . `Regional Rural Banks’ c ould be guided to play its role 
exclusively for Agro and Rural Industries. 
  
20.8  BALANCED REGIONAL   AND NATIONAL ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT. 
20.8.1  Rural industries provide the critical forum n eeded for a balanced regi onal growth due to its 
unique resilient and vibrant qualitie s as a sector which spans the Na tion as a whole. With the secto r
being a combination of traditional skills coupled with modern technology provides a very strong and
potential weapon to combat the nega tive effects of liberalization. It is an accepted fact that in ou r
country, with regional imbalances as they exist, liberalization without the presence of this sector would
have made the existing imbalances extreme and a potent threat to the objectives of rural industrialization
and poverty alleviation. It is in this scenario that this independent Ministry, focusing totally on this
sector, formulating policies to withst and the effects of libe ralization, assumes its critical role in shaping
the national economic scenario. The measures should effectively enab le the achievement of balanced
regional growth. 
20.8.2           The Committees recommends that  the Ministry of ARI s hould take concrete and
concerted and effective m easures for Agro & Rural Industries fo r striking equilibrium   for balanced
regional   growth and overall national economic growth and development. 
20.9  REGULARISATION OF EMPLOYMENT IN AGRO & RURAL INDUSTRIES  
20.9.1  Under the Khadi and Village industries sector so far approximately 63  lakh persons have been
provided employment.  Similarly under PMRY empl oyment upto  2001-02 has been generated to the 
tune of 24 lakhs persons. In the Coir sector about 5.6  lakhs coir workers are being gainfully  employed.

not so pronounced.  However,the Govt. has not undertaken any survey so far in this regard.

REPORT
 
Steel Authority of India (SAIL), the leading steel making company in India and the World’s thirteenth largest steel
producer in terms of crude steel production, is a Company registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1956 and is an
enterprise of the Government of India. SAIL was incorporated in January, 1973 as a holding company for steel and associated
input industries.  From 1973  to 1978, several steel and alloy  manufacturing companies  and iron ore mines were merged into
and  combined with SAIL’s  operation, while the Government of India (GOI) transferred the ownership  of certain consulting,
construction, mining and fire bricks operation from SAIL to other entities. 
 
  The authorized capital of SAIL is Rs. 5000 crore and the paid-up capital of the Company as on 31
st December 2002
was Rs. 4,130.40 crore of which 85.82% was held by the Government of India and the balance 14.18% by the financial
institutions/GDR-holders banks/employees/individuals etc.  The Company recorded a sales turnover of Rs. 15502 crore in
2001-02, however, due to fall in international prices of steel products,  coupled with continued sluggishness in the economy,
the price realization in the domestic market during 2001-02 declined, resulting into the post-tax net loss to the tune of Rs.
1706.89 crore during the year 2001-02.  As a result of loss, the Company has not declared a dividend for the year ended 31
st
march, 2002.  The gross margin (profit before depreciation and interest) and net loss for the nine-months ended 31 st
December, 2002 was Rs. 1334.40 crore and Rs. 545.96 crore respectively.  The company recorded a sales turnover of Rs.
13097.43 crore during this period. 
 
            Global Steel Industry for the measure part of 2001 remained a victim of slow down in demand, sliding price levels,
low realizations, losses and/or falling profits.  However, from the beginning of 2002, the industry entered a recovery phase,
with the gradual firming up of international prices and demand.  During the  financial year 2002-03, the market is signaling an
upward trend.   The year 2003 may well see a price rise in the domestic and the  international steel market.  There have been
price increases in steel products, which have been absorbed by the market.  There has been improvement in production also as
compared to last year and efforts are being made towards achieving maximum capacity utilization matching with the
increased market demand.  The company is vigorously giving greater thrust on the cost control measures during the current
year as well.  With the improvement in market demand, increase in net sales realization and cost control efforts, the company
expects much better results during the financial year 2002-03.
The turnaround in the market trends is reflected most prominently in the performance of the public sector steel giant,
Steel Authority of India Ltd. The unaudited financial results of SAIL for April-December (Q3) 2002 reveals a sharp
improvement in the performance with losses being slashed to Rs. 79 crore in Q3 ’02 - an improvement of Rs. 507 crore over
the corresponding period of the previous year. SAIL’s loss for April-December ’02 was brought to a level of Rs. 558 crore,
showing a recovery of 57 per cent over the results of the same period in 2001. This helped the company to post a cash profit
of Rs 215 crore in Q3 ’02 as against a loss of Rs 297 crore in Q3 ’01 and a cash profit of Rs. 305 crore in the first nine months
of the current financial year.  SAIL had suffered a cash loss of Rs. 434 crore during the corresponding period in the last fiscal.

SAIL markets and sells most of its products through in house Central Marketing Organisation (CMO) which has a
wide network  of 38 Branch Offices and 47 outlets located in major cities and towns throughout India.  International Trade
Division of SAIL looks after export of steel products to countries worldwide.  Raw materials Division manages operations of
key captive mines and quarries  of SAIL.  The captive mines of iron ore and flux meet most of the iron ore requirement and
half of the flux  requirement   of SAIL.
 
SAIL has undertaken major modernization programmes at Durgapur, Rourkela and Bokaro Steel Plants. Under the
modernization programmes, energy efficient Basic, Oxygen Furnace (BOF) technology for steel-making has been adopted in
place of obsolete Open Hearth Furnaces at Durgapur and Rourkela.  Instead of Ingot Casting, Continuous Casting facilities
have been provided in all the three Plants. The modernization projects are being funded from the internal resource of SAIL
without any budgetary support from the Government.  The total investment in modernization of the three plants is likely to be
about Rs. 12,650 crore.
 
 The main objectives of modernization are:

(ii)                Improvement in productivity and yields
(iii)               Reduction in energy consumption
(iv)              Improvement in quality of products
(v)                Reduction in cost of production
(vi)              Reduced environmental pollution

technology; Reduction in cost of production; Pollution Control;  and Improvement in quality of steel produced

STEPSTAKEN FOR TIMELY COMPLETION
 
The Committee was informed that DSP management had taken following steps for timely completion of projects: -
 
(i)
            Close monitoring/follow-up and frequent project reviews at all levels including MD/DSP, Chairman/SAIL and
Secretary (Steel).  Chairman/SAIL frequently reviewed the progress of Modernisation work and took meetings with the
contracting agencies to expedite the work.  Secretary (Steel) reviewed with the contracting agencies once every quarter
and firm commitments were taken from them.  Also, spot decisions were taken to thrash-out the problems.
 
(ii)
            Chasing/follow-up at sub-suppliers’/vendors’ manufacturing works including visits of officials to CIS countries to
expedite strucurals/equipment/refractory supplies.
 
(iii)            Financial assistance/assistance for steel as adjustable advances extended to main contractors in the interest of
expediting progress of supplies/site works and direct payment to some sub-vendors to ensure expeditious delivery of
critical plant and equipment.
 
(iv)            Ensured earliest completion/commissioning of main production units and deployment of DSP’s
operation/maintenance services personnel for erection/cold trial to help expedite hot trial/commissioning.
 
(v)            Rendered continuous help to contractors in planning and monitoring for critical activities.
 
(vi)            Taking over by DSP of a major portion of equipment and part refractory supplied from the scope of TPE Russia for
BF-4 to expedite procurement.
 
The Committee feels that steps taken for timely completion of modernistion package proved inefficient   and   ineffective
as the modernisation projects suffered from time and cost over-run.
