Reasons for Delay
(i)
            Disintegration of erstwhile USSR which resulted in delays in supply of imported structurals, equipment, refractories
etc. from TPE, Russia and affected BF, BOF, SP & RMHC packages.
(ii)            Delays in equipment and structurals  supply by indigenous suppliers affected most of the packages.
(iii)            Increase in quantity of work in respect of civil & structurals job for BF, SP and RMHC packages as compared to
original estimates of the consortium resulted in extra time for execution.
(iv)            Inadequate mobilization of resources at site work by contracting agencies resulted in slow pace of work as compared
to targets.
(v)            Funds constraint of contracting agencies and intra-consortium disputes resulted in slow progress in major global
packages.
 
The DSP management stated that prior to disintegration of the erstwhile USSR, all the economic activities in CIS Nations
were controlled from Moscow and the manufacturing units and transporting authorities had to adhere to the delivery schedules
and commitments.  Subsequent to the break-up of USSR into different Nations, these manufacturing units were being
controlled by different authorities and a number of new regulations were introduced.  This resulted in delay in  manufacturing
activities.  Tyazhpromexport (TPE)’s job has suffered seriously, resulting in delays in supply of imported equipment,
structures and refractories from Russia for four global packages viz, Blast Furnace, Sinter Plant, Basic Oxygen Furnaces and
Raw Material Handling Complex.

Rourkela Steel Plant was initially set up with a capacity of 1 million tonne per annum (Mtpa) of ingot steel in 1960-61
with German technical assistance. The capacity of the Plant was expanded to 1.8 Mtpa in 1969.       The main units of RSP
upto 1.8 Mtpa stage were Coke Ovens, Blast Furnaces, Steel Melting Shop, Rolling Mills consisting of Hot Rolling Mills &
Cold Rolling Mills, Electric Sheet Mill and ERW Pipe Plant. The Special Plate Mill and SW Pip~ Plant were installed later in
1976. Further, a Silicon Steel Mill, consisting of Cold Rolled Non Oriented (CRNO) and Cold Rolled Grain Oriented
(CRGO), was added in Oct'84 and Apr'89 respectively. The main saleable products of RSP are Plates, HR Coils & Sheets, CR
Coils & Sheets, Galvanised Sheets, Tin !Plates, ERW Pipes, SW Pipes and Silicon Steel Sheets.  While the 1 Mtpa stage Plant
operated, more or less, satisfactorily by reaching its rated capacity in 1964-65, the expanded capacity could never be
achieved. The best production level of 1.5 Mtpa of ingot steel was achieved in 1976-77 after which the production capacity
deteriorated. The unsatisfactory performance level was attributable to various factors like deteriorating and inconsistent
quality of raw materials and technological obsolescence. Various studies were carried out to determine the manner in  which
the optimum performance level of the Plant could be achieved. Based on these studies, a scheme for "Renovation &
Technological Upgradation"
(Modernization) of the Plant was considered.
 
The Modernisation of Rourkela Steel Plant was approved by the Government in Oct'89 at a cost of Rs.2461 crores
with FE Component of Rs.396 crores (Base date: 4th Qtr. 88). Government further 'approved in May'92 the revised cost
estimate (RCE-I) of Rs.3954 crores with FE Component of Rs.714 crores (Base date: 1 st Qtr. 92). The revised cost estimate
(RCE-II) of RSP. Modernization works out to Rs.5105.29 crore (FE: Rs.706 crore) on base date of 2nd Qtr'99.

  Modernisation Of Bokaro  Steel Plant
 
            Bokaro Steel Plant, conceived in 1959, is the fourth steel plant among the integrated steel plants in the public sector.
The Plant was conceived in 1959 as a 4 MT plant right from the conceptual stage, 1.7 MT being an intermediate stage for the
project. The construction work for the project was started in late Sixties and the Plant went into commercial production in
1972 with the commissioning of its first Blast Furnace. Steel making adopting the BOF route began a year later. The
downstream facilities -Slabbing Mill, Hot Strip Mill and Cold Rolling Mill were put into operation in stages. The. 1.7 MT
stage was completed in 1978 with the commissioning of third Blast Furnace. The work of 4 MT Expansion was. taken ~p
simultaneously and was progressively completed by Nov'90.     The entire steel making process of Bokaro Steel Plant was
based on the Ingot Casting route which was a technology prevalent in late Sixties. Considering the  various advantages of
Continuous Casting as regards to yield improvement,  conservation of energy and improved quality, Govt. of India sanctioned
Stage I  Modernisation of Bokaro Steel Plant in Jul'93 with a commissioning schedule of Jul'97. All major contracts were
awarded in 12 months. Trials for the Steel Refining Unit were started in Sep'97 and the first Continuous Casting Machine
started its trial runs in Nov'97. Subsequently, all units of Stage I Modernisation have been completed by Jan'00. With the
upgradation of the Hot Strip Mill, the quality of the finished products is of international standard and is being well accepted in
both global and domestic market. As a flat product plant, Bokaro's products include a wide range of Hot Rolled and Cold
Rolled Coils, Plates and Sheets, Galvanised Sheets and Black Plates, serving the needs of railways, tube makers and
automobile industry , L.PG cylinder manufacturers, defence and Petro-based  Industry etc. Quality conscious Bokaro is also
concerned with customers' satisfaction.
 
Approval & Implementation
 
The Modernisation (Phase-l) of Bokaro Steel Plant   was approved by the Government in Jul'93 at a cost of Rs.1625.79
crores (Base date: 1st Qtr.'93) with FE Component of Rs.283.50 crores. The revised cost (RCE-I) of Rs.1792.90 crores (Base
date: 1st Qtr.'94) with FE Component of Rs.301 crores was approved by the Government in Aug'94. The revised cost estimate
(RCE-II) of BSL Modernisation works out to Rs.2468.18 crore (FE: Rs.420.77 crore) on base date: 3rd Qtr.'98.

                  Financial & Business Restructuring in SAIL
 
A number of steps were initiated to combat the declining profitability. The Govt. of India also approved a financial and
business restructuring package  to improve the cost competitiveness of steel industry. While, the financial  restructuring
measures are aimed at mitigating the financial risk by improving the Company’s debt servicing capability, the business
restructuring measures will provide a long term competitiveness in its core business of carbon steel.
 
The financial restructuring of SAIL comprises of:
 
(i)
                  Waiver of loans advanced to it from Steel Development Fund (SDF) to a value of Rs.5073 crores and Rs.381
crores from the Govt. of India.
(ii)                Provision of Govt. Guarantee with 50% interest subsidy for loan and interest thereon of Rs.1500 crores to be
raised by SAIL from the market to finance reduction in manpower through Voluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS).
(iii)               Government guarantee for loan and interest thereon of Rs.1500 crores to be raised by SAIL from the market
primarily for meeting repayment obligation on past loans during 1999-2000.
 
Business Restructuring Envisages:
 
Divestment of  non-core assets while protecting jobs of existing employees.

and steam generating capacity of 660 MT/hour at BSL.
(iv)              74 MW captive power plant  (CPP II) at BSP Bhilai.

The captive power plants at Rourkela, Durgapur, Bokaro and Bhilai have already been divested, with NTPC as the partner for

The sale value of these Power Plants was Rs. 1061 Crores and the capital gain achieved was Rs.777 Crores.

A new incentive scheme with higher weightage to Cost, Quality and Profitability has been implemented w.e.f June 1, 2001.

effectiveness.

year) and 185 Branch Key Accounts (BKA – with contribution potential Rs. 5 crores or more per year) have been identified.

Managers and PIC/PAC have been identified for each key account.

        CHAPTER I
Introduction
1.         When ceasefire was declared with the Naga insurgents in 1964, the Government of India made a commitment to ensure rapid
industrial development to wean people of Nagaland away from violence. The Paper Mill Project was conceived in Nagaland in the late
60s. Nagaland Pulp and Paper Company Limited was incorporated in 1971. This was first and only large & medium unit in the State of
Nagaland and the first paper mill in the central public sector in the North Eastern region. It generated great hope and enthusiasm among
the people of Nagaland. This project was conceived with the following technical specifications:
(i)
                  Capacity : 100 Tons per day i.e. 33000 tons per annum
(ii)                Product : Writing and printing paper
(iii)               Basic Raw Material : 60% Bamboo, 40% Reed
(iv)              Power Requirement : 13 MW
(v)                8 MW to be generated internally from waste head of boilers, 5 MW to be supplied from State Grid
(vi)              Hindustan Paper Corporation, A Central PSU executed the project.
(vii)             Entire responsibility of management rested with HPC.
1.1       The local people donated 700 acres of land for the mill and housing colonies in Tuli area of Nagaland. 126 sq. kilometers of
bamboo forest land was purchased for captive plantation and was leased to NPCC. Water from river Melak was harnessed for water
supply to the Mill. In anticipation of demand from the mill, large scale bamboo plantation took place in private lands.
 
1.2       The project took 10 years to complete. Paper machines for both lines of production were imported from Sweden. Boilers were
supplied by Walchand Nagar Industries. The mill started making commercial production in 1982 with defective boilers. One of the
boilers failed in the trial test and insufficient heat from the remaining boilers kept the Turbine Generator (TG) set idle. The Mill
primarily depended on power supply from the State which accessed power from Assam grid. Thus, the power supply was unstable
besides being costlier.
 
1.3       The defective boilers crippled performance of the mill. The envisaged 60% captive power from Turbine Generator set was not
available and hence the capacity utilization was poor, ranging between 3% to 19%. One of the two production lines i.e. Reed Line was
never utilized. Peak capacity utilization reached 60% on some days whenever power supply was stable. The mill continued to make
losses due to under capacity utilization. The production was abruptly suspended in 1992 as the net worth of the company was eroded and
it was declared sick. Subsequently, it was referred to BIFR in 1992.
 
1.4       The operating agency i.e. IDBI framed a revival proposal and recommended – (1) Capital restructuring; (2) Operation at 60 TPD;
and (3) Fresh investment of Rs. 16.5 crore. Government of India accepted the proposal as approved by the BIFR and it was taken out of
purview of BIFR in 1996. Government of India carried out capital restructuring but did not infuse fresh funds except for VRS, hence

production could not be resumed and it was again referred to BIFR in 1998 for the second time. IDBI was again appointed operating
agency and a Draft Rehabilitation Scheme (DRS) was submitted by them which recommended revival at 60 TPD, fresh investment of 55
cores, other reliefs and concessions applicable to new industrial units in the North Eastern region  and a marginal viability was
envisaged. Nagaland Government agreed to support DRS for its share of reliefs and concessions and fresh investment. However,
Government of India declined to support this Scheme. The decision of Government of India was conveyed to BIFR who in turn asked
the IDBI to advertise for change of management. Although IDBI advertised for change of management, no expression of interest was
received. This position was conveyed to BIFR and thereafter the matter was taken up by Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) who decided
to take a fresh view.
1.5       An Expert team consisting of Hindustan Paper Corporation, Central Pulp and Paper Research Institute and State Government
officers was sent to determine the technical viability of the Scheme. The team recommended revival at 120 TPD of value added paper for
technical and economic viability and an approximate investment to the tune of 150 crores. The MHA directed to carry out the Scheme by
outside consultants. Outside consultants were identified. The cost of detailed project report was to the tune of 30-35 lakhs. The
Department for Development of North Eastern Region agreed to meet the cost of project. However, BIFR refused to grant any further
time and issued orders of winding up.
 
1.6       However, it is worth mentioning that infrastructure development over the years in Nagaland was favourable for revival of the
company. The details of the development are as under:
·
                    Railway line extended to Tuli
·                    Upgraded to broad gauge
·                    Kohima-Mokokchung-Tuli-Amguri road upgraded to National Highway
·                    66/33 HT transmission lines extended to TULI
·                    TULI transformer upgraded from 1.6 to 7.5 MVA
·                    Power availability improved by commissioning 75 MW Doyang and 24 MW Likhimro hydel projects
·                    Substantial investment for road connectivity of Tuli with rest of the State.
 
·                    Coal and Limestone available within a radius of 250 kilometers
·                    Communication and transport facilities many times better than 30 years back.
 
1.7       In the circumstances stated above, the following options are there:
·
                    Wind up and spend Rs.107 crore for closure.
·                    Revive and let HPC manage with the existing arrangement
·                    Revive and privatize as a going concern
 
            Revival is the most feasible and desirable option also compatible with Central Government policy on sick PSUs.
1.8       The matter relating to NPPC was raised by the Members almost in every meeting of the Department related Parliamentary
Standing Committee on Industry when Demands for Grants came up for discussion.  The management of HPC constantly informed the
committee that the company has become non-operational due to insurgency problem in Nagaland.  The Ministry of Heavy Industry also
in their annual reports routinely stated that the company, which came out of the purview of BIFR due to financial restructuring again
became sick as the revival scheme could not be put into operation due to law and order problem, lack of infrastructure and absence of
banking facilities.
1.9       The Committee has been noting over the past years the stereotype statement of the HPC as well as the Ministry of Heavy
Industry.  Law and Order situation has been cited as a major cause for the non-revival of the company.  In this context, the committee
noted that the President of India in his address to Parliament on 25
th February 2002 had said “ The peace process in Nagaland has been
strengthened with satisfactory progress of talks with various militant groups.  What is specially heartening n the last one year is that
people of Nagaland have come out strongly in favour of peace, dialogue  and development, often by staging spontaneous mass

activities”.  Since law and order situation appears to have improved in Nagaland, the committee felt that a beginning may be made
towards reviving NPPCL for the benefit of the people of Nagaland.

Department for Development of North Eastern Region, Railway Board, Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion, Chief Secretary,
State of Nagaland, representatives of Hindustan Paper Corporation, Nagaland Pulp and Paper Corporation, Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd.
and Gas Authority of India Ltd. to explore the possibility of reviving the Nagaland Pulp and Paper Company.  Members of Parliament of
the State of Nagaland also attended the meetings as special invitees.  The date-wise details of the meeting are given below.
 
Meeting held on 15th April 2002
2.1       At the outset, the Sub-Committee-III heard the Secretaries, Department of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises, Department
for Development of North Eastern Region, Chief Secretary, Nagaland, and CMD, Hindustan Paper Corporation, regarding revival of
Nagaland Pulp and Paper Company Ltd.
 
2.2       After hearing the Secretaries of the concerned departments and the Chief Secretary Government of Nagaland, the Committee
recommended that the State Government and employees of the Nagaland Pulp and Paper co. Ltd. should make an appeal to AAIFR
before whom the case was pending for grant of stay.  The committee further recommended that simultaneously, the HPC would call for
bids from the reputed consultants and place an order for preparation of a Detailed Project Report.  The Secretary, Department for
Development of North Eastern Region, assured the committee that his Department would bear 50% of the cost of preparing the Detailed
Project Report.  Secretary, Department of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises, also agreed to meet the balance 50% of the cost.  The
sub-committee observed that after preparation of the Report, the sub-committee would examine the viability of reviving the said
company and thereafter it would request the Government of India and Government of Nagaland to help the company.  The sub-

Ltd.

2.3       At the outset, the Convenor wanted to know the status of the revival scheme of the Nagaland Pulp and Paper Company Ltd.
(NPPC).  Secretary, Department of Heavy Industries, informed the Committee that in pursuance of the directions given by the
Committee at its meeting held on 15 th April 2002, an appeal against BIFR’s decision on closure of NPCC was filed by the Government

industry were appointed on April 22, 2002 for preparation of a Detailed Project Report.  The consultant was to give a Preliminary

2.4       At the outset, the Convenor recalled that revival of Nagaland Pulp and paper Corporation was important because Government of

CHAPTER III
Observations/Recommendations
3.         After hearing the Department of heavy Industry, Department for Development of North Eastern Region (DONER) and Hindustan
Paper Corporation, the committee understands that the main question relates to funding the project and this aspect is to be made clear
before the AAIFR in its next hearing to be held on 1 st July 2003.  It is clear that the NPPC is to be wound up if funding of the project
does not take place.  The committee, however, understands that the Government did not take the revival of NPPC seriously.  This is
corroborated by the fact that on NPPC’s first reference to BIFR, Government of India carried out capital restructuring without infusing
fresh funds except for VRS.  Moreover, the Ministry of Home Affairs appointed a team of experts for the revival of the company.  That
team recommended revival at 12 TPD of value added paper for technical and economic viability with an investment of Rs.150 crores. 
The Ministry of Home Affairs decided to carry our detailed project report and DONER agreed to meet the cost of DPR, which was to the
tune of Rs.30-35 lakhs.  In spite of this, BIFR refused to grant any further time and issued orders for winding up.
3.1       This shows that the case was not properly presented before the BIFR.  When the Ministry of Home Affairs decided to appoint a
consultant to explore the viability of the project, what prompted BIFR to issue orders to wind up the company without going into the
merit of the case, is not understood.
3.2       The DONER has been created for the development of North Eastern Region but it cannot contribute funds for NPPC from non-
lapsable pool as their mandate is to aid only new projects.  In fact, DONER should be made a model agency for the development of the
North Eastern Region, which should encompass not only new projects but also the existing units if any meaningful role is to be played
by the newly created department. DONER should play a leading role for the development of the North East in coordination with
concerned central ministries to usher in real development of the North East.  The Committee notes that out of Rs.1600 crores non-
lapsable pool for North East, Rs.550 crores goes to the budget of DONER for creation/completion of last mile projects in social
infrastructure.  The committee feels that the balance fund may be tapped for funding revival of the company.
 
3.3       The Committee notes that the cost of closure is Rs.107 crores.  In addition Rs.112 crores worth of investment is sunk.
3.4       It has been the committee’s stand that the greenfield fresh project emphasis is from the point of view of Government’s writing off
the loans.
 
3.5       In the light of the views expressed by the HPC, Central Pulp and Paper Research Institute and Economic Advisor to DHI on how
to make the company viable, excise duty exemption for 25 years coupled with transport subsidy should be made available to the
company.  NPPC should also have assured supply of bamboo for a period of 15 years.
3.6       The committee took up the case of NPCC as the peace process in Nagaland is going on and industrial development of Nagaland
should go hand in hand with the peace process.
In case NPPC is wound up the immediate impact would be –
-
                     Colossal waste of all investment made in infrastructure
-                     Serious erosion of credibility of Central Government in sensitive border area.
-                     Wrong signals to ongoing peace process
-                     accentuate already alarming unemployment situation
-                     Nagaland would be wiped of the map of large industries of India.

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having   been  authorized  by the Commi ttee, hereby present this  One hund
twenty seventh Report on the  MoU performance in respect of PSUs of Shipping Industry pertaining to the Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises.  
  
2.         The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry considered and adopted  the Draft report at its meeting held on the  18th August, 2003. 
  
  
CHAPTER - I 
MOU SYSTEM 
1.         The Memorandum of Undertaking (MOU)  is a negotia ted document between the Government, acting as the owner of Public Sector Enterprise (PSE) and a specific
PSE. It contain the intentions, obligations and mutual responsib ilities of the Government and the PSE. Further, MOU makes an at tempt to move the management of PSEs
from management by controls and procedures to management by results and objectives.  
OBJECTIVES OF THE MOU SYSTEM  
1.1       The objectives of the MOU system are to improve the performance of public enterprises by increasing autonomy and accountability of the management; to remove the
fuzziness in the goals and objectives of the enterprise  to pursue through clearly laid down performance targets   in the  MOU and to enable the evaluation of managerial
performance through objective criteria and provide a mechanism to reward good performance through performance incentives to stimulate improved performance.  
1.2       Under the agreement the enterprises undertake to achieve the targets set in the agreement at the beginning of the yea r. Thus the MOU covers both financial
performance as well as non-financial performance. Under this syst em performance of the company is categorized into five categori es namely: excellent,very good, good, fair,
and poor. 
THE GENESIS OF MOU SYSTEM 
1.3       The genesis of the policy of Memorandum of Understa nding can be traced to the report of the Arjun Sengupta Commitee. One of the recommendations of this
Committee was for the introduction of the system of MOU for measurement of performance of public enterprises. The MOU system wa s introduced on an experimental basis
in 1987-88. It was based on the French system. From 1989-90 the signaling system was adopted and it remains in vogue till now. 
One of the most important difference between the French system and the signaling system is the possibility of making an overall  judgment on the enterprises performance in
the latter system. In the performance contracts belonging to the Fr ench system, one could only point out whether a particular t arget was met or not. This created grea t
difficulty for making an overall judgement regarding enterprises performance. The signalling system overcomes this problem by a dopting the system of "five point scale" and
"criteria weight" which ultimately result in calculation of "composite score" or an index of the performance of the enterprise  
PREPARATION OF MOU 
1.4       Based on the guidelines issued by the DPE in October/November, the draft MOUs are prepared by PSEs and forwarded to t he Administrative Ministry and DPE by

approval, they are signed by Chief Executives and Secretaries.  
EVALUATION 
1.5       The evaluation of the MOU signing enterprises is done at the end of the year by the Ad-hoc Task Force on the basis of  actual achievement vis-a-vis the MOU targets. 
Where the performance exceeds the target by the predetermined sti pulated level the enterprise is ranked as 'excellent' and when  the target is just met, the enterprise is ranke
d
as 'very good'. In other cases, where the targets are not met the enterprise is ranked either 'good' or 'fair' or 'poor'. Ranki ng depends on how the performance has been as
compared to MOU targets. 
1.6     The performance criteria should be assigned appropriate weights corresponding with their stated priorities in the objec tives.  It should be ensured that they also reflec t
the perceived relative importance of the various criteria in th e judgement of the PSE/Ministry.The weight for physical criteria  should be kept as low as possible. Instead,
Efficiency and Dynamic criteria should get higher weights.  The we ight for profit-related financial parameters would be 60% in case of PSEs operating under free marke t
mechanism. The weight of 60% would be dist ributed to,  Gross Margin,  Gross Profit/Capital Employed and   Net Profit/Net Worth,  each having a weight of 20% each. Fo r
PSEs operating under administered prices, PSEs where Government is  sole/almost sole customer & Trading, Consultancy, Engineerin g and Financial PSEs, the weight would
be 40%. The weight of 40% would be distributed to,  Gross Marg in and   Net Profit/Net Worth, each having a weight of 20% each.  The PSEs which have been specially se t 
up for implementing  certain government policy directives will have no pre-determined financial parameters.  
  
  
1.7    The targets set should be realistic and growth oriented. It shoul d be ensured that the MOU targets flow from the Corporate Visi on/Plans formulated by the PSEs an d
there is linkage between them. In case there is any variation, reasons thereof should be clearly specified.        For qualitative indicators, the targets for each of the points on the
5-point scale should be indicated in the performance matrix itself. If these  targets are on a time scale, only such target which fall within the MOU year is  included. 
  
  
1.8       The MOU should contain the past five years' perform ance data on criteria included in the MOU in an appendix. It shoul d also indicate the projections for the next five
years, as far as possible consistent with the corporate plan.  
  
  
1.9       This report on MOU  in shipyard and related industry is an   exercise in the study of memorandum of understanding of  public sector undertakings i.e. Hindustan
Shipyard Limited (HSL), Goa Shipyard Limited (GSL) and Cochin Shipyard Limited (CSL).    The Sub-Committee-III for Ministry of heavy Industries and Public Enterprises 
undertook the study of MOUs  of public sector units in shipyard related industry and visited Goa from 12 th to 15th  January, 2003  in order to have interaction with the 
management of  Hindustan Shipyard Ltd. Vishakhapatnam, Goa Ship yard Ltd.,  Goa and Cochin Shipyard Ltd., Cochin and Mormugao Po rt Trust , Goa.  In this exercise, the
Sub-Committee comprehensively reviewed  the Memorandum of Unders tanding of these Industries and endeavoured to shape its  obser vations/recommendations in the ligh t
of the facts/data presented by these PSEs before the Sub-Committee during the visit.   
  
WORLD DEMAND 
1.10     As per an estimate published in the shipping world and shipbuilder July/August, 2001 the  Global order book for Commer cial new buildings    likely to be sustaine d
over the next 10 years as the world fleet of 90,000  Vessels need replacement,  2200 to 2300  ships per year will be required a s replacement to the old ones and to mee t
additional tonnage requirements.  Ship repairs and conversions are also expanding in terms of  global  demand worth around 8 billion dollars a year. 
1.11     As per the report of the subgroups of the working group on SB& SR industry – 10 th  Five Year  Plan, on the global plane, sea borne trade is expected to grow at a 
steady rate of 2.2%  has been  estimated that between 1998-2008, a total  of 198  million  Gross Registered Tonnage (GRT) is pl anned to be built compared to 125 million
GRT built in the preceding decade.   In the world   shipbuilding capacity is consequently expected to grow from 28   million CG T to 40 million CGT  annually.  Similarly,
ship repair activity will grow from 150  million GRT to  200 million GRT to sustain the aging fleets and to meet the emerging environmental norms. 
1.12     Thus the focus on  shipbuilding and    economic performance has gained importance in the  last few years.  China has started making its presence felt in the market and
shipbuilding achieving   is expected to shift to this country in the  near future.  India is expected  to become the next econo mic giant.  Hence there is an urgent need to reverse
the present situation and a policy  is to be evolved at the apex level to promulgate orders for placement of orders by Indian Ship owners on Indian Shipyards for fuller capacity
utilization for the balanced growth.

CHAPTER – V 
  
AREAS OF CONCERN FOR SHIPYARD INDUSTRY 
(I)        Under Utilization of Capacity 
5.         The Hindustan Shipyard (HSL) is  handicapped by the fact that it has got only  one building dock with a capacity to build vessels upto 50,000 DWT.  The level o f
Technology  & Computerization is low and even the design office is yet to be upgraded to international   standards.  HSL mostly  depends for orders from Indian Navy , SCI,
Port Trusts, ONGC, DCI, A&N Administration UTL etc. Lack of   coherent strategy and libealisation in regulatory norm made it ea sier for Indian Ship owners to acquire
vessels from abroad, domestic shipyards industry has lost its clients and does not have requisite  technology, plant & equipment and subsidies at  par with foreign shipyards to
attract new orders. 
5.1       Currently there are three dedicated shipyards, viz. Mazagon Dock Ltd., Garden Reach Shipbuilders & Engineers and Goa Shipyard Ltd.  under  the Ministry o f
Defence  Production who amongst themselves split the requirement of Navy &  Coast Guard leaving    only the spill over, if any,  to non defence shipyards.  The existing
defence shipyards may not be able to cope with  the completion of number of orders of the Defence production programme in the X Five Year Plan.   
5.2       The Committee recommends  that HSL having built &  repaired  various sophisticated vessels including retrofitting/rep air of submarines and having all infrastructure
and human skills/expertise at  par with other Defence yard,   MoU  should be signed  between  I.N.,  Coast Guard & HSL for mutu al benefit and cooperation. Hence
weightage should be introduced in MoU document for cooperation of Indian PSUs for larger benefit of Indian shipyards and HSL in particular. 
5.3       In the  last five  years the Value of Production (VOP) has increased from Rs.111.31 crore in 1997-98 to Rs.220 crores  in the  year  2001-02 .  However it will not be 
possible to sustain this growth if new orders do not materialize in the immediate near future.  The downward trend in the capaci ty utilization has already se t-in.  Situation is 
that, with  the present orders GSL is not in a position to fully  utilize the manpower in the  area of hull construction and outfitting activities.  The overall capacity utilization of
the yard  is about 45.69% in December, 2002.  Since vessels yard 1183 & 1186 will be delivered by March, 2003 , the capacity  u tilization figure will further come down. 
GSL has  expertise and facilities developed  for  medium sized s ophisticated vessels like Missile Crafts and Extra Fast Attack Crafts for  Navy, Fast patrol Vessels an d
Advanced Offshore Patrol Vessels for  Coast Guard/Navy.  If suffici ent orders for  medium sized Naval/Coast  Guard vessels are not received  by   GSL  from esteemed 
customers soon, the manpower & infrastuctural capacity of the yard will remain un-utilised. 
5.4       The Committee observes that under-utilisation of existi ng capacity by GSL  in the absence of work-order is a matter o f grave concern. This negates the prospect o f 
expanding the work sphere of G.S.L. This is also in contravent ion of the performance of the PSU as shown under MoU. The Committ ee therefore recommends that capacity
utilization of a PSU should be reckoned as a vital factor and given due weightage under MoU. 
  
5.5       The Committee was apprised that despite efforts to promote export of Shipyard’s  products and services, it has not be en possible to secure any order because majority
of enquiries require  an integrated institutional   response from the   Indian  side  comprising Shipyards, the Indian navy and  the Government to  ensure  the successful
outcome of promotional efforts besides making funds available for bridging the gap between the order   value and the cost  of  production in the market entry phase.

approved to the  Shipyards for  enabling such activities to be undertaken on a regular basis.  This will enable self-sufficienc y in production/maintenance of products/ships 
serving the defence/nation.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that a concerted effort should be made by shipyards, Indian N avy and the Govt. to ensure successful

(III)     Disposal of Scrap 
5.7       Government  of India  have exempted import of ra w materials, bought out components a nd consumables  required for both  shipbuilding/ship repair duty free.  
Considerable difficulties are experienced in disposing of scrap generated during the shipbuilding process.  As per Sec. 65 2(a)  & (b)  of the customs Act, Scrap generate d
during manufacture of goods are to be valued on the basis of  impor ted  scrap or on the basis of value of parent  material depe nding on whether the manufactured   item has
been  exported or cleared for domestic consumption respectively.  In either  case   the value being realized on disposal of scrap from shipbuilding are much less than the value
of imported scrap/parent material.  As a result the yard stands to lose heavily on sale of scrap.  
5.8       The Committee, therefore, recommends that in order to streamline the procedure the scrap generated may be valued  at rate of realizable value.  Necessary 
amendments to the relevant  sections in the Customs Act are called therefor. 
(IV)     Rationalization of Duties 
5.9       The shipyards  have  been facing difficulties on the excise duty also .  The scrap generated form shipbuilding/ship r epair operations are exempted from Excise duty
since the final product viz. ship building and ship repair activities are exempted.  For effective utilization of yard faciliti es the shipyard often   undertakes  other  fabrication
jobs which are   dutiable in nature.  As per Notification  No.89/95 dt. 18.5.95 of Central Excise  and Salt Act 1944 in case dut iable activities are carried out in an organization
where exempted products are manufactured, the entire scrap gene rated by the organization will attract excise duty.  Accordingly ,  the shipyards stands to lose the benefits o f
excise duty exemption when other works are carried out in the in terest of effective utilization of yard facilities and manpower .    Since separate accounts and records are kept 
for  exempted works,  excisable works scrap arising from exempted works may be exempted from the payment of excise duty  even i f excisable goods are also  manufactured
concurrently. 
5.10     The Committee finds that as existing arrangements, capit al  goods imported for ship repair are exempt from levy of  Cu stoms Duty, whereas the same goods fo r
shipbuilding  are not exempted.  The Committee thereforer recomm ends that since shipbuilding is a capital intensive industry an d margins from new building operations are 
negligible,  capital equipments required for shipbuilding for m odernisation, upgradation and expansion of capacities may be exe mpted from levy of Customs duty as in the
case of ship repair. 
  
(V)       Inter  Public Sector Shipyard Corporation 
6.         Out  of the seven public sector shipyards in the country, three are under the Department of Defence production cater ing mainly to the requirements of Indian
Navy/Coast Guard and other four shipyards in terms  of vessels built, technology employed and work culture,   each shipyard is d istinct from  the other.  For instance Cochin
Shipyard with its modern facilities and systems is capable to build and repair vessels upto 110000 dwt and  125000 DWT, respect ively.  Hindustan Shipyard  has the 
capability to handle vessels of smaller capacities   (upto 40000  dwt).  Wherever, joint efforts to securing orders is feasible  to yield desired results,  will be pursued.
Recognising the potential  for securing sizable business  from the offshore repair sector,  a consortium arrangement has been m ade between Goa Shipyard Ltd (GSL),
Hindustan Shipyard Ltd (HSL),  Mazagon dock Ltd (MDL) and cochin Shipyard Ltd. (CSL).   
  
6.1       The main purpose of  Co-operation is to sustain and improve the capacity utilization of the yard by regular patroniza tion by the  other PSUs, exchange and transfe r
valuable technical and managerial know-how for upgrading productivity and quality of product at each centre  to a level which m eets the requirements without    unhealthy  
competition wishing prosperity to one another and to arrive at innovative solutions for the prosperity of Defence, Maritime  and Oil Sectors.  Also in time of tension and crisis
like war, the role to  be played by Indian Shipyard  for building &  repair of ships, such as Survey vessels, OPVs, Submarines etc. can be  discussed and defined by Indian
navy.  The PSUs can  help co-operate each other by maintaining a competitive  edge in a very depressed market. 
6.2       The Committee  recommends that a weightage factor is to be introduced   in MoU document for cooperation of Indian PSUs for  lar ger benefit of  Indian Shipyards
and HSL in particular. 
6.3       The Committee further observes that in the absence  of  any tax  shield, the Shipyard has to pay Corporate  Tax on it s profits.  Presently, no special dispensation is
available to shipbuilding/ship repair  industry under the income tax act, whereas  Shipping Companies enjoy   special concessions under Sec.33 AC  of the income Tax Act.   
6.4       The Committee  recommends that extension of a sim ilar provision to shipbuilding and repair industry will enable them to plough back profit   for acquisition of new
assets for much needed upgradation, modernisation and expansion projects at  low cost. 
6.5       The Committee recommends that  a consensus on product range should  be developed within each shipyard so as to avoid duplicatio n of design and detaile
d
engineering efforts. In the absence of a well developed marine  infrastructure in the country major part of the raw materials and equipment required  for construction /repair of
vessels are being sourced   from abroad.  There are  only very few manufacturers and limited items that can be sourced from ind igenous market. The Committee recommends
that   items being sourced  from abroadshould  be identified  .  A list of such items being procured from abroad should be made   with specifications earmarked and be given to
domestic suppliers for supply.  The domestic s uppliers  can react to it and present to the Government what hurdle/constrains   they are facing in supply of these items. 
Technology wise they can  seek cooperation and collaboration of foreign companies for joint production. This will pave the way for indigenisation of shipping industry from
mere assembling of parts imported from abroad. It is quite   evident  that shipyards  are strategically  necessary to build and  to maintain  Warship and patrol Vessels to secure
extraction of oil & gas offshore from the Exclusive Economic Zone  and keep the sea lanes safe   and secure.

I N T R O D U C T I ON
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliame ntary Standing Committee on Industry,  having   been
authorised  by the Committee, hereby present this One hundr ed Twenty Eighth Report on  Provisions and Prospects o f
Auto Policy as announced by the Government of India, in March, 2002 pertaining to the Department of Heavy Industry
(Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises). 
2.         The Department-related Par liamentary Standing Committe e on Industry in its 47 th Report on Demands for Grants 
pertaining to the Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public  Enterprises had recommended that the Government shoul d
formulate an Auto Policy.  The Committee in its 59 th Report on  Action Taken by the Government on the 
recommendations contained in its 47th Report stressed that an  Auto Policy ma y be formulated by the Government without
further delay.   In response to the Committee’s coveted re commendations, the Department of Heavy Industry in its Action
Taken Note informed that the Government of India have brought out an Auto Policy on 7th March, 2002. 
3.         The Committee took up the Auto Policy as a nnounced by the Government for detailed discussions in order to
examine the developmental features of the policy and to know  whether the provisions enshri ned in the Auto Policy as
announced by the Government on the reco mmendations of this Committee is in  consonance with the conceived an d
original intention of the Committee and fulfilling the practical demands of the automotive industry of the country in
general. To understand the provisions and prospects of the Auto Policy and its implication on various sectors of economy,
the Committee in its series of meetings  held on 24th June and 16th July, 2002 interacted with the Secretaries of Ministry of 
Heavy Industries, Petroleum and Natura l Gas, Road Transport and Highways, Small Scale Industries, Steel, Power,
Commerce, Finance (Revenue).  
4.         In order to have the in-depth understanding of  the requirement of the automotive industry and to examine whethe r 
the Auto Policy as announced by the Governme nt is fulfilling the expect ations of the automotive industry in general, the
Committee under took study visit to Chennai from 20th to 23rd January, 2003 and interacted with   the Auto Manufacturers, 
Auto Components Manufacturers a nd Tyre Manufacturers.  The Committee in its meeting held on 22 nd May, 2003 hear d 
the representatives of the Ce ntral Road Research Institute, TELCO, Ashok Leyland, LML and Hindustan Motors Limited 
on the subject.  Two study groups of the Committee undertook study visit to Pune and Ludhiana simultaneously , from 23rd
to 26th May, 2003.  The Committee fu rther visited Gurgoan on 27 th May, 2003 and interacted wi th the representatives o f 
Sona  Koya and Hero Honda.  The Committee in its meeting held on 24 th June, 2003 heard the representatives of Maruti 
Udyog Limited, Reva Electric Car Company Limited, HMT (Tractors), Apollo Tyres. 
5.         The Committee also sought the suggestions of Auto Tyre  Manufactures Associations (ATMA) and Society of 
Indian Automobile Manufacturers (SIAM) on the Auto Policy which assisted the Committee in its examination of the Auto
Policy.    
6.      The present report is an effort towards suggesting th e Government for comprehensive Auto Policy for the benefits o f
Automotive Industry fulfilling their expectati ons and actual requirements.   It is expected that the Government would give
due consideration for modificat ion in the Auto Policy for the incorporation of the provisions as suggested by the Auto
mobile manufacturers, Auto Tyre manufacturers and Auto Components manufacturers.    
7.         The Committee is thankful to the representatives of the various Ministries and representatives of organizations who
appeared before the Committee.  The Co mmittee also wishes to thank the various Ministries and organizations fo r
furnishing their replies to the questionnaire and the points raised during the course of   oral evidence.   
8.         The Committee at its  meeting  held on  19th August, 2003 considered and adopted the Report.

OBSERVATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE  
  
APPROACH AND METHODOLOGY ADOPTED   
  
In order to analyze the Auto Policy the Committee adopt ed various approaches and methods. At the outset the
Committee prepared a de tailed questionnaire based on various aspects of the Auto Policy and the questionnaire was 
forwarded to various Departments/Ministries for their commen ts thereon.  On receiving their comments  the Committee
formed its opinion thereon and the replies of the Ministries have been  incorporated in the report at the appropriate place.

The Committee undertook on the spot study visit to understand the impact and implications of the auto policy on
various structural aspects of the automo tive industry through interaction at various levels.  Study visits undertaken by the
Committee provided the opportunities to unde rstand the status of automotive industry, their problems and the response o f
the industrialist to the Auto Policy. At the same time the study visits also provided the opportunity for on the spo t
observation of the industrial situation and thus helped the Committee to analyze and diagnose the prevailing conditions and
circumstances of the automotive industry on empirical-parameters  . The Committ ee took the first hand information from
the industry and thus helped in the collect ion of data from the primary source. On ce the data pertaining to the automotive
industry were collected the same were anal yzed to have diagnosis of automotive industry which helped in identification o f
the problems of the automotive industry and searching the possible solutions.   
  
While oral evidence of various auto manufacturers and auto co mponents manufacturers undertaken by the
Committee  enabled the Committee to have face to face interaction with the captains of the automotive industry.  Problems
of the automotive industry were heard in  detail and efforts were made to find out  the solutions. Direct interview of the
representatives of automotive industry by the Members of the Committee helped in having across the board discussion on
various aspects of the automotive industry.   Oral evidence  of the representative of automotive industry were recorded an d
the same were used while formulating the report.   
  
            The Committee made its efforts to study the Sectoral -specific status of automotive industry.  Analytical an d 
descriptive methodology was adopted to understand the problem s of various segments of  automotive industry i.e.
manufacturing (Two-wheelers, Three – wheelers, Cars, Tractors, Multi-utility Vehicles, Commercial vehicles).  
  
While analyzing the various segments of the automotive industry the Committee could arrive at a conclusion tha t
Auto Policy must address the various segments of the automotiv e industry i.e. to say the Auto Policy must be sectoral-
specific.   
  
            The Committee also took the help of “compara tive analysis approach”.  For example in manufacturing segments 
the Committee made its efforts to unders tand the Auto Policies of leading countri es in Car manufacturing.  On various
places data relating to automotive industry in India have been compared to the gl obal context in order to have in depth
understanding of the relevance of the Auto  Policy in the national and the global c ontext.  Comparative analysis approach
helped the Committee to understand the st ages of actions required for impleme nting the Auto Policy, the mode o f
implementation – mechanism, timing and duration of a programme of the Auto Policy and the specific segments fo r
implementation of specific course of actions.  
  
            The SWOT analysis  (Strength, Weakness, Opportunities and Threats) adopted by th e Committee intended to
understand the automotive industry in its tota l environment.  It help the Committee with the existing policies and practices
of the automotive industry, identification of the problems of the various segments  of automotive industry in mega, micro
and relevant environment.  While the mega environment helps in unde rstanding the technological and economic
environment of the automotive industry at the domestic and gl obal level, the micro environm ent helped in understanding
the industry specific environment and the Committee arrived at a conclusion for recommendi ng specific course of action
for specific segment of automotive industry.  By the relevant  environment the Committee restricted the scope of its search
for exploring the opportunities of the au tomotive industry for a better tomorrow  as well as finding out the safeguards
against the possible threats of automoti ve industry.  It is through identifyi ng the strength and opportunities of the
automotive industry the Committee have been able to pin point  the Government the “Key Areas for Massive Action”, to 
achieve the objectives of the Auto Policy  by strategic managerial decisions and adhering to the principle of Managemen t
by Objective (MBO).   
  
            The Committee also adopted the holistic appro ach.  After studying the various segments of automotive industry the
Committee made its efforts for tailoring the various segments as a whole. The Committee tried to co-relate the various 
allied sector of the automotive industry i.e. R&D, Banking, In surance, Road Safety, Auto Fuels.   The Committee made its
efforts to have an integrated approach  for understanding the automotive industry a nd to find out ways and means i.e. co-
operative and collaborative attit ude of various allied sectors of automotive industry for the betterment of the automotive
industry.  It is by adopting this approa ch the Committee came to the conclusion th at inter sectoral c ooperation is required
for the future growth and development of automotive industry.

            Automotive industry has universally emerge d as a significant driver in the economy in the liberalized an d
globalized economy.   Because of the inhe rent strength of automotive industry’s li nkages with down stream industries, its 
role becomes pivotal in the country’s economic and industrial development.   The well-developed automotive industry, 
with deep forward and backward linkages, ably fulfils this catalytic role by producing a wide variety of vehicles: passenger
cars, light, medium and heavy commercial vehicles, multi-utility vehicles such as jeeps, scooters, mo tor-cycles, mopeds, 
three wheelers, tractors etc. 
  
            The automotive industry in India is nearly six decades old, until 1982, only three manufacturers – M/s.  Hindustan   
Motors,  M/s.  Premier Automobiles and M/s.  Standard Motors dominated the mo torcar sector.  Owing to low volumes, i t
perpetuated obsolete technologies and was out sync with the world industry.  In 1982, Maruti Udyog Limited (MUL) came
up as a Government initiative in colla boration with Suzuki of Japan to es tablish volume production of contemporary
models.  After the lifting of licensing in 1993, 18 new ventures have come up of  which 17 are for manufacture of cars. 
Besides the 17 manufactures of cars I ndia has 9 manufactures of commercial vehicles, 14 of 2/3 Wheelers and 10 o f
Tractors and 5of engines. 
  
            The automotive Industry comprising of the au tomobile and the auto component sectors has made great advances
since delicensing and opening up of the sector to FDI in 1993.   The investment in the i ndustry is Rs. 50,000 crore up to
31.3.2000.  The turnover the of automob ile industry exceeded Rs. 63,025 crore in  2000-2001.  Including turnover of the 
auto-component sector, the automotive industry’s turnover exceeded Rs. 81,600 crore approximately.  The industry
provides direct employment to 4.5 lakhs and generates indirect employment of 1 crore.  The contribution of automotive
industry to GDP has risen from 2.77% in 1992-93 to 4.0% in 1998-99.

lower overheads.  The demand from the OEM market, on the other hand, is dependent on the demand for new vehicles.

and above.  The industry made a beginning in 1961 with a to tal production of 880 units.  There has been a substantial

have introduced higher Horse Power tracto rs of 75 HP with imported components for meeting the specific requirement o f
high HP category of tracto rs.  The production of tractors in the range of 31-40 HP is around 60%, in the range of 41 HP 
and above is 23% and below 30 HP categor y is 17% of the total production.  Traditionally, Haryana, Punjab and Utta r
Pradesh are the main States for the tracto r market.  The new markets for tractors in the States of Madhya Pradesh, Andhra
Pradesh, Tamilnadu, Maharashtra and Gujarat States are growing at a faster pace.  
  
The auto sector (excluding Tractors ) attained a steep cumulative annual growth of 22% between 1992 and 1997. 
The Tractors achieved a cumulative annual growth of 16% .  Component production grew by 28%.  There has been a
slowdown in the automobile sector in the past two years.  However, the component industry maintained a low but positive
growth rate mainly due to its export pe rformance.  Over the year s, the component industry has maintained a 10% - 12% 
share of exports in the total production.

Industrial Policy-Automotive Sector:- 
  
            Automotive sector is a delicensed sector.  As  such, no licence is required for setting up a new unit except when a
unit is being set up within a periphery of 25 kms of a city  having population of more than one million.  Since July 1991
when new Industrial Policy was announced, the automotive sector was covered in  priority sector i. e. automatic approval
was being granted by the RBI for foreign equity up to 51%.  Government approval through FIPB was necessary for foreign
equity beyond 51%.  However, now even 100% foreign direct investment is being allowed through automatic route by RBI
since January, 2000.  Government approval is necessary only in some exceptiona l cases in case of FDI.  Automatic
approval is also granted by the RBI fo r foreign technology agreements where th e lumpsum payment does not exeed Rs. 7
crores (US $ 2 million) and royalty does not exceed 5% on domestic sale and 8% on expor ts.  Government has furthe r
liberalized the technology transfer agreem ents and now royalty is being allowed by 100% wholly owned subsidiary to the
parent company.  Quantitative Restriction on imports have been lifted from  1.4.2001.  DGFT has issued notification fo r
regulating the import of new and old vehicles taking into account the environmental and road safety. 
  
  
OBSERVATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 
  
            Having gone through the status of automotive industry in I ndia, the Committee finds that Indian auto industry has
the potential to become a key growth dr iver of the Indian economy.  Indian automobile industry has since long been 
governed by regulations.  Imports, collabor ations and equity ventures were re stricted by the Government.  Capacity
expansion was restricted and required licenses were issued by the Governme nt.  Technology transfer from foreign
companies and payments therefore were al so restricted and subject to Government  approval.  However, with the onset o f
liberalization and globalisation process, the global automotive industry is on the move, therefore, the domestic automotive
industry needs to catch up with pace of gl obal development.  For this to be achieved the Government needs to play a more
active role in developing this industry.  The policy levers adopted so far by th e government do not pr ovide a sufficiently
strong support framework to the industry play ers.  Other countries seem to have no t only clearly stated goals, but also a
more comprehensive and coherent  approach to policies.  Successful devel opment of the auto industry in other countries
reveal several principles  for effective policy.  India needs a more proactive auto polic y, for India to achieve the industry
vision. Such an effective auto policy ha s to target the specific needs of each  segment of the industry depending upon its
maturity level and competitiveness.

OBSERVATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 
  
The Committee observes that in the nascent stage of the au tomobile industry, Government regulations and policies
typically have the objectives for increasi ng the size and growth prospects of the industry, deepening the industry, both in
terms of supply base, and forward linka ges and finally improving technological and human capabilities.  Almost all
countries have used government policy as the key driver for developing a world class automotive industry.  The strategies
have varied from restructuring of the industry, incentivising technology transf er, fostering growth to encouraging
investment decisions.               
  
            The Committee further finds that the Indian automotive policies have been a mixed record of successes and failures
in the past.  Currently except for the MoU policy for passenge r cars, concerning which seve ral issues were highlighted,
there is no explicit policy for ot her segments.  In addition to these issues was the historical bias against the car segment,
manifested in high excise duty.  Fina lly countries which had successfully gr own their auto industry to near global
competitiveness had several char acteristics, which seem to be missing in the Indian auto policy.  Foremost among them
being an overall driving objective.  It is in this background that the Committee st rongly recommended in its 47 th and 59th
Report that to harness the full potential of the automotive industry, India requires a comprehensive auto policy.  A coherent
growth oriented policy will not only expand the industry considerably, it will al so increase the competitiveness of the local
industry and generate higher le vel of employment.  However,  policy framework will depend on the specific needs of each
segment to meet the vision. 
  
CHAPTER – IV 
  
VISION, OBJECTIVES AND MEASURES OF AUTO POLICY 
             
Vision Statement 
  
The vision document of auto policy declares to establish a globally competitive Automotive Industry in India and to
double its contribution to the economy by 2010.  
  
Objective         
  
The Committee has been apprised that the Auto  Policy as announced by the Government on 7 th March, 2002 aims 
to promote integrated, phased, enduring a nd self-sustained growth of the Indian automotive industry.  The objectives are
to:- 
  
(i)      Exalt the sector as a lever of indus trial growth and employment and to ac hieve a high degree of value addition
in the country; 
(ii)    Promote a globally competitive automotive industry and emerge as a global source for auto components; 
(iii)   Establish an internationa l hub for manufacturing small, affordable  passenger cars and a key centre fo r 
manufacturing Tractors and Two-wheelers in the world; 
(iv)  Ensure a balanced transition to open trade at a minimal risk to the Indian economy and local industry;

Government is planning to undertake some measures to  realize the policy objectives.  The Committee has been

Foreign direct Investment  
  
            Automatic approval for foreign equity investment upto 100% of manufacture of auto mobiles and component is 
permitted. 
  
Import Tariff 
  
            The auto policy proclaims that the incidence of import tariff will be fixed in a manner so as to facilitate
development of manufacturing capabili ties as opposed to mere assembly w ithout giving undue protection will ensure
balanced transition to open trade; promot e increased competition in the market a nd enlarge purchase options to the Indian
customer.  The Government will review the automotive tari ff structure periodi cally to encourage demand, promote the
growth of the industry and prevent India from becoming a dumping ground for international rejects. 
  
            In respect of items with bound rates viz. Bu ses, Trucks, Tractors, CBUs and Auto components, Government will
give adequate accommodation to indigenous industry to attain global standards. 
  
            In consonance with the objectives of the Auto Policy, in respect of unbound items i.e., Motors Cars, MUVs,
Motorcycles, Mopeds, Scooters and Auto Rickshaws, the import tariff shall be so designed as to give maximum fillip to
manufacturing in the country without extending undue protection to the  domestic industry. 
  
            The condition for import of new Complete ly Built Units (CBUs), will be as per Public  Notice issued by the
Director General Foreign Trade (DGFT) having regard to environmental and safety regulations. 
  
            Used vehicles imported into the country w ould have to meet CMVR, environm ental requirements as per Public
Notice issued by DGFT laying down specific standards and other criteria for such imports. 
  
            Appropriate measures including anti dumpi ng duties will be put in place to check dumping and unfair trade
practices. 
  
EXCISE DUTY 
  
Motor Cars 
  
            The ownership of cars in India is just 6 per thousand of population as against 500 in the developed economies.  The
contribution of the auto sector to th e GDP and employment is likewise low.  Expansion of local demand holds grea t
potential and is vital to install scale volumes of production. 
  
            Domestic demand mainly revolves around small ca rs not exceeding 3.80 meters in length.  Small cars occupy less
of road space and save on fuel.  These capture more than 85 % of the market.  India can build export capability and become
an Asian hub for export of small cars.  The growth of this segment needs to be spurred. 
  
Multi Utility Vehicles

            MUVs are an important mode of economic al mass transport in rural India due to poor road infrastructure and lac k
of good State transport system.  They are the first vehicle pur chased by a number of farmers, traders, small businessmen in
rural and semi-urban markets.  The Government will endeavour  to provide fiscal incentives to this sector. 
  
  
Commercial Vehicles 
  
            Presently excise duty on commercial vehicles sold by a manufacturer whether as a chassis or with a complete body
is 16%.  However, no duty is levied on the body that is built by an independent body builder on chassis bought from a
manufacturer.  This dispensation inveigles production of the complete trucks a nd buses by the chassis manufacturer and is
detrimental to safety standards.  The duty imposed on the construction of bodies by an i ndependent body builder, small o r
organized sector, shall be equal to that of bodies built by a chassis manufacturer. 
  
            The Government will encourage fabric ation of bus body on bus chassis de signed for better passenger comfor t
instead of truck chassis which is in practice. 
  
            The Government will  promote the use of multi-ax le vehicles for carriage of goods as they cause reduce d
environmental pollution and lesser wear and tear on road surface in comparison to the existing 2-axle trucks.  
  
Improving Road Infrastructure 
  
            Traffic on roads is growing at a rate of 7 to 10% per annum while the vehicle populati on growth for the past few
years is of the order of 12% per annum.  Poor road infrastructure and traffic c ongestion can be a bottleneck in the growth
of vehicle industry.  A balanced and coordinated approach will be undertaken  for proper maintenance, upgradation an d
development of roads by encouraging priv ate sector participation besides public investment and incorporating lates t
technologies and management practices to take care of increase in vehicular traffic. 
  
            For the convenience of traveling public the Government shall also  promote multi-modal transportation and the 
implementation of mass rapid transport  systems.

pattern over a period of time rather than a separate deci sion on the issue in an adhoc fashion.  The Committee furthe r
believes that the vision statement of a policy must entail the scenario of the issue involved  over a considerable period o f
time.  Measuring the auto policy as announced by the Government on this criteria it seems that the vision of the policy is
not far-sighted.  The auto policy merely sets a target for doub ling the contribution of automotive industry in the economy,

comparative analysis of the domestic and global auto industr y scenario, the Government should come forward with the 
auto policy for the period of 20 years.

with global technology standards even in the domestic market.  Taxation and other policies should therefore be engineered
to promote higher levels of technology.  When this happens, industry will be forced to offer higher technology levels even
to domestic consumers in order to remain competitive in the market.  Resultantly indi genous component manufacturers
will become familiar with global technologies and global quality expectations.  This will raise the credibility of India made
automobiles in global markets and make them more acceptable to internationa l consumers.  In reality convincing
customers to buy Indian Automobileswith European safety or emission norms will not be credible as long as Indian
domestic market norms are far below those that we are atte mpting to export.  Demonstrat ed familiarity with global
technology standards will be essential to prove Indian auto manufactu rers’ credentials in a global market.  It is suggeste d 
that Government should actively promote early adoption of global technology and standards by providing import duty an d
excise duty concessions on products adapting such technology and standards before they are mandated.  
  
Promoting Real Indigenisation 
  
            An automobile industry of truly global ca pabilities needs bedrock of a str ong and technologically vibrant auto
components sector.  Most manufact urers in India have paid only lip service to  the cause of the component sector.  These
are many segments of the component industry that are truly world class, but many MNC ma nufacturers keep them out on
specious plea of little consequence only in order to promote component im ports from vendors in the mother country.  The
present import tariff regime completely supports such an approach.  Under WTO also obviously nothing much can be done
to promote real indigenisation.  There is however a variety of non-tariff appr oaches that can be taken in this regard.  
Insurance can be used to promote indigensition.  Presently insurance on new cars is levied ad-valorem basis, irrespective of 
what a claim costs an insurance company.  Typically cars w ith higher real indigenisation le vels have lower spare parts
prices.  Therefore, a policy that reward s lower parts prices will work to encour age indigenisation.   Vehicle insurance
charges should be related to the observed cl aim cost brand wise/model wise  or to the price of a basket of spares typically
consumed in insurance claim cases.  In the present situation owners of cars with lower claims ratios (&lower spares prices)
are in effect subsiding those with higher ratios.  Most private sector entrants in the general insurance sector, as a policy, do
not cover such cars with high spare prices.  Only PSU insu rance companies do.  The IRDA has consistently adopted an
anti-consumer stance by not  allowing free pricing of motor car  insurance.  It has allowed insurance companies to cartilise
in the name of regulation.   Free pricing of insurance will ensure that cars with the lowest claim ratios either through higher
indigenisation and lower parts prices or through better safety-related technology  will attract lower insurance.  This will in-
turn encourage both indigenisation and te chnology upgradation.  Another non-tariff measure to aid the development of a

the global passenger car market there is  enough headroom for rapidly growing de mand with the help of a facilitating
Government policy. Since the passenger car  segment of the Indian automotive indus try is the least mature segment and is
plagued by low demand, high fragme ntation and high acquisition cost, the auto policy needs to re-orient and redress the 
passenger cars to focus on the growth of passenger car segment for commercial harnessing  of  the growth drive r

paradigm.  One of the key determinant of demand is acquis ition cost, which is primarily based on sale price and curren t
income levels.  The acquisition cost in I ndia for passenger cars, in terms of months  of median salary required to purchase
the most popular passenger car, is one of the highest in th e world. Moreover,  50% of th e acquisition cost of a passenge r
car is due to taxes.  This co nsists of excise duty, import dut y, sales tax, insurance and regi stration tax.  As passenger cars
are considered luxury items, the relative tax is much higher than commercial vehicl es or 2-wheelers or even other durable
goods.  The current level of taxation may seem comparable to other countries in percentage terms, but since, taxes
represent over 20 months of median dispos able income, they constitute a major de terrent to demand.  It is a fact tha t
developing countries favour commercial vehicles with a lower ta x rate verses passenger cars, in the development stages o f
the economy. At present there is a bias in the taxation structure against passenger cars in India.  This has resulted in a much 
higher commercial vehicle to pass enger car sales ratio in India compared to global levels. (In India it is 60% compared to
global sales mix of 31.5%).  
  
            The Committee is of the view that the policy maker, while formulating the policy for the passenger car, has to keep
the global trends for passenger car.   The global auto ma rket is mature and competitive.  In the post liberalized an d
globalized economy, only countries which are integrated into a regional econo mic  block (EU, NAFTA, MERCUSOR,
ASEAN) have been able to achieve signi ficant level of exports due  to comparative advantages and regional supply chains
of OEMs, e.g. Brazil (MERCUSOR), la rge domestic market and Mexico (NAF TA), Czech Republic (EU) low labou r
rates.  India will thus find it difficult to create an export market (or even significant level of exports) driven car industry  at
current levels of domestic capability and demand base ma inly because of lower and decreasing domestic protection
available to the industry under WTO, low current technology base, absence of integration with any regional block SAARC
regional block is not happening, moreover, it is too small.   
  
            However, the Committee feels that to ac hieve the vision of making auto se ctor 10% of industrial production,
passenger cars will have to be the key.  The passenger car segment, which currently accounts for only one-third of the auto 
industry output, will have to grow at a rate  of about 16 per cent per annum in real terms, to contribute about 40% of the
auto industry output.  As is the case in other economies, which are using auto industry as a grow th driver (like Malaysia,
Indonesia etc) passenger car industry output has to grow from the present level of Rs.125 billion to Rs.725 billion by 2010
or from the present level of 400,000 units to close to 2.4 million units.  Given the current rate of per capita income growth
and income elasticity of demand 1.6, the market size will grow to 1.5 million by the year 2010.  So as to reach the target of
2.4 million, the industry as well as the Government need to ta ke initiatives to reduce price,  increase quality and provide
better value to the consumer, improve road infrastructure as well as encourage replacement demand. 
  
            The Committee believes that the opportunities for growth are maximum in passenger cars.  Globally, passenger car
segment is the biggest segment of the auto industry acc ounting for over 4 times the volum e of commercial vehicles. 
Passenger car industry tends to be the product and process technology driver for the manufacturing industry.  Passenger car
sector has a significant multiplier impact due to its widespread forward and ba ckward linkages in the economy.  Passenger
car industry has been the driver  for rubber, plastics, telematics, financing and numerous other industries.  In the auto
industry passenger car segment is the segm ent, which has a truly global supply ch ain and world class products that will
enable India develop an industry that is quality and cost competitive.

vision of making passenger car globally competitive.  The industry needs to focus on domestic markets along with
developing global competitiveness, therefore, the following course of action is suggested:-

            The Committee recommends that the Government  needs to take the initiative of preventing the import of secon d
hand cars and MUVs into India as well as facilitate exports.  Duty s hould be levied on the market  price in the destination
country and not on the market price in the country of source.  The policy should ensure that the tari ff barriers are effective
in dissuading imports of used MUVs.  This can be achieved by ei ther moving towards 8 digit level of harmonization or by
negotiating a higher bound rate for import of vehicles and using the higher dut y level for second hand cars and MUVs. 
Additionally, stringent safety and emission norms should be applied. 
  
            In regard to the scrappage of vehicle be yond economic life, the Committee observe s that to meet the challenges o f
low replacement demand, high air pollution from in-use vehicles, low acceptance of  better technology, outdated 
transportation practices,  the Government should allow a one-time scrappage of old ve hicles in a pre-defined window of 3-
5 years (latest by 2004) for renewing the utility vehicle populati on in the country.  Moreover, vehicles which have crosse d
their economic life, and which cannot be easily maintained in ‘Fit’ condition need to be forced out of the road by law.  The 
Committee is of the view that the Governme nt should give a one time fi scal incentive  i.e. concesional excise duty or roa d
tax exemption for sale of ut ility vehicles against scrappi ng of more than 15 year old vehicle.  The Committee furthe r
recommends that the policy should ban usage of more than 20 years old vehicle all over the country otherwise, there will
be a flourishing market for vehicles ove r 15 years old vehicles in smaller town s and upcountry areas, and the scrappage
incentive scheme will become ineffective. 
  
TWO WHEELERS SEGMENT 
  
            The Committee is pleased to observe that the India has th e second largest two-wheeler market in the world, which 
has enabled the industry players to reap the benefits of econom ies of scale. Two wheelers se gment is the most mature an d
competitive segment in the auto industry, however, exports as a percentage of domestic demand, are still negligible.  The
Japanese have been pioneers of the two- wheeler market.  Currently, all the majo r markets for two-wheelers other than 
India are dominated by Japanese manufacturers or Japane se-affiliated manufacturers.  Chin a, which is the biggest market
for two-wheelers, is completely dominated by Japanese fi rms, either through joint ve ntures or technology transfe r
agreements. 
  
            The Committee believes that in order to achieve the vision of maki ng auto sector 10% of the industrial production,
the two wheeler segment will have to grow to over 13 million units.  This will require product design/quality
improvements along with market push to ensure that two-whee lers remain the most popular vehicle of choice.  The vision 
is achievable given the past growth ra te of 10% in volume terms.  Even if the domestic industry continues to grow a t
historical growth rates, the domestic demand will be over 11 million units by 2010.  The balance is targeted to be me t
through exports i.e. 2 million units per annum by 2010, whic h will have to reach 20% by 2010 if the vision is to be
achieved. 
  
            The Committee recommends    the following strategies to achieve vision target for two-wheeler segment :- 
  
(i)      Improve the current product quality, range  and features to meet internati onal standards in terms of quality, 
emission and product features. 
(ii)    As Indian firms push into global ma rkets, they can no longer depend on in ternational players with whom they
compete, for product and process technology.  Consequently, they will need to develop indigenous
capabilities for world class product and process design.  The most importa nt critical challenge would be to
develop capabilities to design products suited for targ eted export markets rather than find markets which
suit Indian products.  For example, it is imperative to  bridge the technology gap in  terms of reliability an d
consistency in performance which is driven by both design as well as manufacturing excellence. 
(iii)   To achieve the vision target of 13 million units, Indian players will also have to aggressively focus on exports. 
Given that the key markets which already have strong local players, Indian players will need to eithe r
differentiate their product or target new export markets,  like Latin America, Africa etc.  this will require
massive investments by the Indian Players in sa les and marketing along with setting up extensive
distribution and service network. 
(iv)  As majority of countries, including India are becoming environment conscious, Indian players need to invest in
development of clean and fuel efficient two-wheelers. 
  
The Committee further recommends that the Government should facilitate the negotiati on of bilateral agreement 
for allowing free trade between India and some key markets like, Pakistan, Ch ina and Africa etc. (the proposed free
movement with SAARC/ASEAN can give a thrust to exports) and to initiate a Market Development Fund for brand-
building and enabling distribution of Indian products.  Simil arly, the Government needs to facilitate the import o f

(i)      Incentivise independent auto design firms to set up shops in India by providing them tax breaks and duty
concessions. 
(ii)    Incentivise Indian OEMs and component suppliers to si gnificantly increase their R&D expenditure for a well
